#10653. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10650. 5 signs you are not going to be made obsolete by AI

It is difficult to open any newspaper (I know, who still does that anyway?) or consume any news, let alone join any business discussions, without having to talk about AI. The topic does not go away, though within this broad topic there are so many layers and subthemes and messages that it rarely gets boring, anyway.

As Garrison Lovely noted in his brilliant book, Obsolete, people tend to fall into three categories when it comes to AI attitudes. There are the accelerators, who are basically in the utopian camp and accordingly convinced that artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, so we cannot go fast enough in our efforts to accelerate and evolve AI. At the opposite extreme, we can find the worriers, who think AI-induced human extinction is looming and even if not, there’s a strong chance that AI will have devastating effects on work and life. And then you have the critics who are broadly skeptical about most popular claims about AI, whether positive or negative, and perhaps most controversially believe that AI is simply overrated.

Since nobody has data on the future, we will avoid picking camps here—time will tell, and by “time” we should really mean the next two or three decades rather than 2027 or 2028. Indeed, obsessing over the future can be an unhealthy strategy for not dealing with present problems and concerns, including how to remain relevant in an age in which AI is unquestionably performing a large number of “knowledge economy” tasks that were hitherto the exclusive remit of human intelligence. As I predicted in I, Human, AI’s growing ability to compete with human skills is not just redefining what it means to be human, but also forcing us to double down on the things AI cannot replace even in order to remain employable.  

Key indicators

So, how should you assess your employability and career success in today’s AI age, and what are some positive signs that you are unlikely to be automated or made obsolete by AI? As of today, here are five critical indicators to consider:

(1) You have a “messy job”: As Luis Garicano at the London School of Economics wisely noted, one of the best ways to resist automation is to have a chaotic, unpredictable, or “messy” job. Indeed, AI’s value is mostly in automating tasks, but you can only automate what you can standardize first; conversely, if you automate chaos you get chaos at scale. This is not to be mistaken for having a disorganized or chaotic mindset, which makes even predictable and orderly things seem chaotic, but rather an objectively unpredictable, complex, and nonrepetitive working routine—or if you prefer, a nonroutine!.

(2) You have a “hungry mind”: As my colleagues and I showed, contemporary careers require not just a strong work ethic and people skills, but also high levels of intellectual curiosity. Indeed, this is even more pressing in the AI age, which removes incentives for developing or harnessing human curiosity—why learn, after all, if you can answer any question at your fingertips just by prompting genAI? In that sense, you can think of genAI as the intellectual equivalent of the fast food industry. It’s there 24/7 and provides you with a tasty, quick, cheap but not very nutritious fix, and it can be quite addictive too. Just like our hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t need standing desks, gym memberships, or Pilates (for they were active all day and only ate very healthy and nutritious food . . . IF they were active enough to procure it!) it is conceivable that their offspring may need to develop new cultural adaptations in order to keep their mental muscles from atrophying. For example, they may go on “thinking retreats” to stimulate those parts of the brain that have become nearly dormant because every thinking task is outsourced to AI. Until we get there, curiosity will keep some people more active in the thinking and learning departments, and for them there is hope. (Incidentally, this will also allow them to understand and leverage AI more, including for augmentation purposes.)

(3) You are entrepreneurial: While employers are trying to figure out what AI will do to their organizations and jobs, some people are finding ways to leverage AI’s disruptive and innovative potential. Not so much to delegate boring and tedious tasks—typically, the value AI brings is not in what it automates, but rather what humans learn to do with the time they save—but in order to experiment and test new ideas and innovations. In essence, entrepreneurial people see opportunities where others don’t, and they are quicker than others to act on those potential opportunities by bridging the gap between demand and supply. For example, in the AI age, a single individual can now launch a business that would previously have required a small army of employees, using AI to conduct market research, develop products, build websites, create marketing campaigns, manage customer relationships, and even provide customer support. Likewise, professionals can turn their expertise into new products and services, identify unmet customer needs, or experiment with business models that would have been too expensive or time-consuming to test before. In that sense, AI is not just a tool for doing existing things faster or cheaper, but an opportunity to do things that were previously impossible, or at least economically unviable. The critical difference, of course, is that while AI makes it easier than ever to execute an idea, it does not necessarily make people better at coming up with good ideas in the first place, let alone identifying which ones are worth pursuing.

(4) Your employer is seriously committed to “augmentation” rather than “automation”: Most organizations promise their employees “augmentation dreams,” which roughly translates into a utopian world where their jobs are more interesting, fun, and rewarding, and they are more productive because they have AI as their copilot or co-intelligence. However, many of these employers give up on the vision and instead yield to the temptation to automate and cut entry level jobs just to show some ROI from AI. Fortunately, some employers have not given up yet. You may consider yourself fortunate and less vulnerable to automation if your employer is genuinely trying to figure out how to augment rather than automate humans in the AI age. As always, choosing your employer (and boss) wisely is often more consequential for your career than whatever skills, personality, or talent you may have.

(5) Artificial general intelligence is less likely than techno-enthusiasts think: As Garrison Lovely explains in Obsolete, much of the debate about AI’s impact on humanity rests on assumptions about the future that are presented as if they were facts. In particular, the notion that AI will inevitably progress from today’s impressive but imperfect systems to artificial general intelligence (AGI), capable of matching or surpassing humans across virtually every cognitive domain, remains a prediction rather than an established scientific fact. Indeed, there is a rather significant difference between building machines that can perform an ever-growing number of intellectual tasks and creating machines that can think, reason, learn, and adapt as flexibly as humans do, particularly in unfamiliar situations. Of course, this does not mean AGI is impossible, or that we should dismiss the very real risks of AI simply because some of its most enthusiastic advocates have a tendency to confuse science with science fiction. Nor does it mean that AGI is necessary for AI to displace millions of workers. However, the assumption that human intelligence is merely a temporary competitive advantage, destined to disappear as soon as machines become sufficiently powerful, is far from proven. In that sense, perhaps the most reassuring sign that you will not become obsolete is that nobody, including those who are most confident about predicting our obsolescence, actually knows when, whether, or how AGI will arrive. And while betting your career on the failure of technological progress would be unwise, betting against the accuracy of Silicon Valley’s predictions may be a rather more sensible strategy.

Ultimately, the best way to avoid becoming obsolete is not to obsess over what AI may or may not be able to do in the future, but to focus on what you can do today to remain valuable, relevant, and adaptable. This means cultivating the skills, mindsets, and opportunities that enable you to work with AI rather than compete against it, while remembering that your employer’s choices may matter as much as your own. Even if AI stopped evolving today (which, let’s face it, is unlikely), we would still need to work hard to upgrade ourselves as humans, especially to be future-fit for an employment market that has already been shaken up by AI.

#10649. The memo was never the point. The point was to clarify your thinking

In 2004, Jeff Bezos banned PowerPoint from Amazon’s senior leadership meetings in favor of narrative memos, read in silence at the start of each meeting. The idea was that a well-structured and tightly argued memo communicated its ideas in a way that a deck built around bullet points could not. As Amazon moves into the AI era, it is developing internal tools that can help produce polished documents much more efficiently. Its internal AI assistant, Cedric, promises to deliver “six-page narratives in seconds,” according to Kristi Coulter, a former Amazon executive.

But no matter how good Cedric’s outputs are, using an AI tool to trim the traditional writing process down to mere seconds undercuts what made well-written memos valuable in the first place. The memo itself was never the point. What mattered was what writing the memo forced the human to do. As Bezos put it, there is “no way to write a six-page, narratively structured memo and not have clear thinking.” The process, not the output, was the real source of value. 

How AI breaks the memo

Bezos wasn’t promoting writing for its own sake. Writing mattered to him because it was a forcing function for rigorous thinking about important decisions. As one Amazon veteran told Coulter, writing the memo forced them to confront their own ideas and clarify what they wanted to say. And this often meant that writers would change their mind several times while writing the narrative.

It is true that building meetings around memos disciplined the readers as well. Because meetings began in silence, everyone worked through the same argument before anyone spoke, and the discussion started from the substance. But if the content of a memo carries less of the writer’s thought, the value of reading it diminishes in proportion to that fall. Time spent studiously reading well-written but empty texts is time wasted.

The underlying problem is that AI can break the link between thinking and the production of text. Steve Huynh, a former Amazon principal engineer, recently described a review meeting in which a product manager began discussing a six-page memo he was supposed to have written. Almost immediately, it became clear that he was reading it for the first time. He was presenting something that he had not thought about at all.

Readers are adapting to the change in the writing process. Coulter reports that one Amazon manager now asks for longer documents because he plans to have AI summarize them, and Huynh says some employees now tag suspect memos “AI;DR”: AI, didn’t read. In a Stanford and BetterUp Labs survey on workslop, 42% of workers who had received low-effort AI-generated work said they saw the sender as less trustworthy. Once a written product stops being evidence that someone thought about the content, readers simply stop giving it their attention.

The memo’s 3 jobs

The trap for leaders is to treat this as a problem about memos. Ultimately, businesses don’t need memos. They need good decisions. The memo mattered only because, for a long time, it reliably communicated the results of the thinking process that lay behind the writing.

Baseball provides a useful analogy here. In his book Moneyball, Michael Lewis tells the story of how the Oakland A’s responded to the loss of a star player, Jason Giambi, to free agency. Instead of trying to replace him with another player of the same caliber, the A’s realized they didn’t need another Giambi, per se. What they needed was the measurable impact he had on their results. So rather than search for one player to fill the gap, they tried to recreate him “in the aggregate” by finding several cheaper players who together delivered the same statistical impact.

There is a lesson here for how we think about Amazon’s memos—and, indeed, for how we think of much else in the new AI-powered workplace. We shouldn’t be looking for simple substitutions of AI work for human work. Instead, we should look at how work produces value in aggregate and then redesign workflows to reproduce the end result, not the individual steps. 

A well-written memo bundles three distinct jobs into one artifact. It forces authors to think, it provides evidence that the author has done the thinking, and it gives its readers a shared understanding of the issue at hand. What the Oakland A’s can teach us is that, rather than trying to restore all of those functions in one stroke, the better path is to make two distinct moves: one that restores the first two jobs together, and one for the third.

Force the thinking, then prove it

The rebuilding process starts with honesty about where thinking is actually needed. A great deal of human writing does not provide the basis for making important decisions, so in those cases there is little reason to build a replacement process that forces the thinking and evidential functions alongside the communicative role of the writing. A report summing up project progress over the past week, for instance, can simply be an assemblage of information, and the process of collating and communicating it can happily be automated. But when it comes to visions of the future or arguments about which decisions are best, leaders have to adapt to the fact that polished prose no longer guarantees deep thinking.

The first move is to both rebuild the forcing function and provide evidence of the underlying thinking. This can be done by making the author, rather than the document, the thing that gets examined. Amazon’s meetings already included the seed of this requirement. Once the silent reading ended, the writer had to answer for every line. The change for the AI era is that the defense becomes the initial gate. A memo earns its place on the agenda only if its author can walk the room through the argument and take questions without the document in front of them. That is not something the author can hand to Cedric, because Cedric will not be in the room, and knowing the defense is coming does what the blank page used to do. 

Terence Tao, the Fields medalist, has proposed the same rule for mathematicians: If the authors of an AI-assisted result cannot give a clear, expert-level talk on it, the result should not be published. A proof that no human can properly explain, he writes, “should be viewed as incomplete, even if it has been formally verified.” The same holds for a memo.

Who does the understanding?

The memo’s third job, helping create shared understanding, seems the least problematic, but it raises a counterintuitive challenge. We tend to think that AI-written texts are problematic because they waste our time by spreading poorly thought-out ideas. Restoring the underlying thinking should, then, automatically solve the communication problem as well. But things are not quite so clear cut. Even when the content is genuinely good, AI can help humans produce more valuable outputs than other humans can absorb.

We can see this in the challenges that the discipline of mathematics is facing. Mathematicians are being overrun by journal articles and preprints containing AI-generated proofs that nobody can properly digest. In September, OpenAI said its models had solved one of math’s Millennium Prize problems. A month later, it released hundreds of AI-generated results in one batch. Many of the proofs have been verified by software that checks their logic, but knowing that a result is correct is not the same as understanding why it is. The Association for Human Mathematics put it bluntly in a statement reposted by Tao: “We reject OpenAI’s assertion that this release advances our subject.”

Pavel Etingof, a mathematician at MIT, argues that AI’s results truly become part of mathematics only when a human reads them, understands them, and gets something out of them. A thousand new proofs sitting unread on a shelf add nothing to the discipline. The same logic holds for companies grappling with a surfeit of good writing outputs; no matter how intelligent a memo is, it becomes a part of a company’s decision-making only if the relevant humans absorb it. That points to a new division of labor: AI can increasingly shoulder the generative burden, but the understanding still has to be done by people.

That makes human understanding a scarce and valuable resource, and leaders may have to start rationing it. Working out how to filter and direct the flow of outputs becomes an entirely new type of task. The preprint server arXiv, for scientific papers, now limits authors to two submissions a month. A company can do something similar, such as limiting the number of memos that get a silent-reading slot in a given month.

The artifact is not the thinking

For two decades, a six-page memo was reasonable evidence that someone had thought hard. AI has broken that link, and no policy will fully restore it. What leaders can do is stop mistaking the document for what it was meant to produce. The alternative is more six-pagers than ever, and fewer people who understand what’s in them.

#10647. Motorola Signature 27 specs detailed in new video, including Tandem OLED display

Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs.

A video hands-on from Danny Winget on YouTube offers a closer look at Motorola’s upcoming flagship, and only makes its arrival all the more enticing.

There are several key specs mentioned in the video, with the most interesting being the “Extreme AMOLED Duo” display which makes use of Tandem OLED technology. Tandem OLED isn’t a new idea, with the tech stacking multiple layers of diodes on top of each other to improve contrast and brightness. Tandem OLED can be found on Apple’s new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, as well as 2024’s Honor Magic 6 RSR. But Motorola’s use of it in the Signature 27 is certainly nice to see, especially given the other spec shared. 12,000 nits of brightness. That rather insane figure is apparently the peak brightness on this new flagship.

Hardware shots of the phone also show the textured backs on the two color variants as well as the curved glass around the display.

I think it’s a interesting phone with a good camera system. But it also depend on the price. Anyway nice to see Motorola compete in the flagship space again.

The battery capacity isn’t revealed, but Winget says that it is “sizable.” Similarly, the vapor chamber is described as “40% larger” but a point of comparison wasn’t given.

It’s all shaping up for a powerful flagship in every sense of the word. Motorola has confirmed that Signature 27 will launch on November 5, and I don’t know about you, but I’m only getting more excited about it.

#10646. How the New Urbanism took on sprawl and won

It’s 1996. You just moved to a suburb of Atlanta, to a roomy house on a quiet street. Every morning at dawn, you kiss your family goodbye, and then hop in your car to drive 35 miles to your office in the city. It takes more than an hour to get there. 

You have plenty of company on the road at that hour, as you’re one of the more than 600,000 people who moved to the northern outskirts of Atlanta over the last six years. Between the traffic and constant construction, the swelling suburbs are starting to show their fault lines.

Its rapid growth during the 1990s makes Atlanta the quintessential story of suburban growth gone awry, though it is far from alone. Between 1950 and 1990, the share of Americans who lived in suburbs jumped from 23% to 46%. Decades of post-World War II expansion had transformed the American landscape from one built around small-scale neighborhood development and center city density to tabula rasa growth on the edge. Families moved to cul-de-sac subdivisions spread across car-dependent exurbs. These places were not so much cities as they were lily pads of domesticity, linked together by steadily growing interstate highways.

For many Americans, a suburban lifestyle was an outward signal of success: big house, good schools, safe streets. But that wasn’t the case for everyone. In the 1990s, at the peak of suburban sprawl, a small but vocal group of detractors began to take shape. Comprising progressive urban planners, designers, architects, and policymakers, this group coalesced around the idea that there should be an alternative way to live—one that embraced the charms of small town centers, the convenience of walkable neighborhoods, and the diversity of mixed-use and mixed-income districts. 

These people would come to be known as the New Urbanists.

In 1996, the New Urbanists wrote a 27-point charter that laid out its core principles for better city planning. At a gathering in Charleston, South Carolina, a line of 262 people ceremoniously walked up onto a stage and signed their names to the charter, legitimizing once-fringe ideas as a new kind of rule book for neighborhood design and city building. Signatories included architects, urban planners, transportation engineers, and government officials, from unknown environmental activists all the way up to the U.S. secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

Over the past 30 years, the charter and its principles of planning and design have gone on to radically change the face of cities and communities across the U.S. and around the world. New Urbanism has grown into a nonprofit organization, the Congress for the New Urbanism, and a movement that’s changed the way cities are planned and built, upending rigid zoning laws, eliminating parking minimums, and bringing walkability back into the hearts of communities. 

The objectives of New Urbanism still resonate today, and have been gathering new currency in the face of worsening housing affordability and growing disappointment with mainstream urban design priorities. The abundance movement, inspired by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s book Abundance, calls for a proactive approach to economic and social development that can affect everything from the supply of housing to renewable energy access. Similarly, a recent push by Stripe’s cofounder, Patrick Collison, and the libertarian economist Tyler Cowen aims to spur the creation of “new aesthetics” that can change the course of cities and the architecture within them. Post-Great Recession, post-COVID-19 pandemic, there is an evident hunger for change.

Anyone now arguing for reimagining cities can take lessons from how New Urbanism emerged and rose to prominence. Three decades after the historic charter signing, Fast Company spoke with the people who were most involved in creating the New Urbanism movement—all still alive, all still working—about how such an unlikely crusade took hold. In a rare retrospective, they look back on how their movement took shape, and the legacies of sprawl that New Urbanism is still fighting today.

Roots of a design movement

The New Urbanism didn’t appear out of nowhere. Its roots grew out of a mix of disillusionment and optimism that started taking shape in the 1970s. At that time, a small group of young planners and architects were starting to feel fed up with the built environment. They believed that many of the social and environmental issues cities faced were the result of development patterns that prioritized economic returns over the experiences of the people who lived there. 

With highways expanding to reach new subdivisions and new subdivisions arising alongside new stretches of highway, the traditional logic of urbanization was being supplanted by a perverse pattern of growth for the sake of growth. How people lived in these places, what they did there, and why they’d even want to be there were seemingly irrelevant. The environmental costs of populating these areas and keeping them going were afterthoughts at best.

A group of young designers believed development needed a more comprehensive, interdisciplinary, and thoughtful approach, and they set out to show how it could work. They included the Miami-based urban planners Andrés Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, the Los Angeles-based architects Elizabeth Moule and Stefanos Polyzoides, and a regional planner in California named Peter Calthorpe. Now all in their 70s and 80s, their paths began crossing after coming out of various architecture and design programs in the 1970s and working as architects and planners across the country.

“We began practicing when the collapse of suburbia became evident. The promise of suburbia, which was plenty of green, plenty of parking, highways that really work, was betrayed,” says Duany, cofounder of Duany Plater-Zyberk & Co. (now DPZ CoDesign). “You didn’t get nature. You got a whole bunch of traffic congestion in commuting, and all the great parking fields were miserable places. So there was a feeling of betrayal in the air and we were able to perceive it.”

After studying under the influential architectural scholar Vincent Scully, Duany and Plater-Zyberk graduated from Yale University in 1974 and moved to Miami, where they cofounded the architecture firm Arquitectonica, and then, in 1980, Duany Plater-Zyberk & Co., a firm focused on counteracting suburban sprawl. 

Calthorpe had also studied at Yale but left in the mid-’70s before graduating to work under the California architect Sim Van der Ryn, who in 1975 was appointed state architect by Governor Jerry Brown. During Brown’s administration, Calthorpe worked on a new plan for downtown Sacramento built around a burgeoning light rail system, an early example of transit-oriented development, which would become Calthorpe’s specialty.

Meanwhile, Moule and Polyzoides had started an architecture firm in Southern California centered on bringing traditional architectural approaches to housing beyond the typical single family home, designing courtyard homes and clusters of housing that would, decades later, become known as “missing middle” housing.

“All of us were working on parallel paths from the mid-’70s on,” Calthorpe says.

Those paths began to intersect in the 1980s as the designers’ alternative takes on urban and suburban development garnered more attention. An early standout was Seaside, a Gulf Coast resort town in Florida planned by Duany and Plater-Zyberk and founded in 1981. The pastel-toned walkable village-like development, later made famous as the set of the 1998 film The Truman Show, is considered the first New Urbanist community. 

“We were architects who were networking. There was a lot of travel to give lectures in the world of architecture about the latest things people were working on. And we realized there were people around the country that were heading in the same direction,” says Plater-Zyberk.

In 1986, Calthorpe and Van der Ryn published a book called Sustainable Communities, which outlined emerging elements in the planning and urban design fields that were changing the shape of cities. It included case studies of places that were designed to reduce resource consumption and lessen reliance on cars, as well as a focus on utopian-leaning new town development. Later, Calthorpe was teaching a course on transit-oriented development at the University of California, Berkeley, with the architect and urban designer Dan Solomon, who would later become one of the founders of New Urbanism, and they invited Duany to participate in a symposium on new forms of suburban development.

Slowly, the individual and varied work of these practitioners would intermingle. “We were working on different sides of the same coin,” Calthorpe says.

The founders coalesce

By the beginning of the 1990s, the future founders of the New Urbanism movement joined forces. Their first real meeting was around a plate of pasta.

During Calthorpe’s time working under Governor Brown, California had enacted new energy efficiency and building standards, and created a statewide organization called the Local Government Commission to spread best building practices out to all the jurisdictions across the state. Run by Judy Corbett, a pioneer in sustainable development, the commission had a role that was interpreted broadly. Around 1990, Corbett saw an opportunity to tie energy efficiency to larger neighborhood planning, land use, and transportation issues.

“Judy called me up and said, ‘I want to get some design principles that are clear and firm, but something I can pass around to elected officials throughout the state of California,’” Calthorpe recalls. Duany and Plater-Zyberk were in California working alongside Moule and Polyzoides on the Los Angeles redevelopment project Playa Vista, so Corbett and Calthorpe organized a meeting. They saw the chance to use California’s push for energy efficient buildings as an opening to get more people thinking about ways growth and development should change. “We all met in Judy’s kitchen in Davis, California, and had a pasta dinner and talked about shaping some kind of movement,” Calthorpe says.

“I don’t know that we thought so much as being a rebellion as much as feeling like we were profound outsiders and the forces in front of us that were creating the cities that we live in were remarkable,” Moule adds.

This led to Corbett’s organizing a Local Government Commission-led conference at Yosemite National Park’s historic Ahwahnee hotel in 1991, bringing together architects, planners, transportation engineers, government officials, and policymakers from across California. Calthorpe, Duany, Plater-Zyberk, Moule, and Polyzoides helped drive the discussion.

Moule recalls that during the meeting they created a rudimentary series of tenets called the Ahwahnee Principles that helped define their thinking at different scales, from the building block to the street, neighborhood, district, and region. The principles called for planning “complete and integrated communities,” with a variety of activities, housing types, and jobs, and designs that conserve resources and minimize waste. 

“We knew that if we put a little bit more meat on the bones and fleshed them out a little bit more, and then gathered people together to see what they thought about it, then we might be able to get somewhere,” Moule says.

The group agreed that the Ahwahnee Principles should be considered a starting point for a large-scale rethinking of the developer-led, piecemeal urban development patterns of the previous decades. “We were talking about it and saying, you know, these principles are right but they’re not going to get us there. We need more detail. We need to be more specific,” Plater-Zyberk says. “It was one of the things that pushed us to make our own group that was urban design oriented, with greater detail or depth than planning and much more specific goals.”

Around this time, Duany was having discussions with the architect Léon Krier. A harsh critic of modernism, Krier was the future master planner behind the New Urbanist town of Poundbury, England, initiated in the late 1980s by Prince Charles (now King Charles III). Krier, who died in 2025 at 79, impressed on Duany how modernist architects had had such a deep influence on 20th century architecture and urban planning through a formal organization called Congrès Internationaux d’Architecture Moderne (CIAM), founded in 1928. He suggested the anti-sprawl movement needed its own formal organization.

“I was aware of just a few colleagues that were on the same page. And we basically called them,” Duany says.

Calthorpe says Duany proposed a group that would “repeal and replace” CIAM. “They had congresses and they issued a charter. So we thought, well, we’re going to do exactly the same thing. We can just cut and paste, take out the bad shit and put in the good,” Calthorpe says.

New Urbanism’s first congresses

Around 1992, Duany, Plater-Zyberk, Moule, Polyzoides, and Calthorpe gathered in New York, along with a planner named Peter Katz, who was working on a book about new approaches to urban planning and design (The New Urbanism: Toward an Architecture of Community, published in 1994). The six discussed the overlapping intentions of their design and planning work, and what it would look like to bring a more interdisciplinary approach to creating a more livable urban environment.

“We started with nothing, just fumes,” says Polyzoides, cofounder of Moule & Polyzoides Architects and Urbanists, and now dean of architecture at the University of Notre Dame. “There was so much to learn. There was so much to unveil, really, because the subject is so deep.”

From their work, they knew that reimagining the built environment would be a complicated undertaking. Interrelated forces shape the world as we know it, from land use planning to neighborhood design to traffic engineering to natural resource consumption. Making wholesale change hinged on understanding and reforming how all those interrelated pieces fit together. They walked away from the meeting with a plan to break everything down to three scales: the regional, the neighborhood, and the building. They also came up with a name for themselves: New Urbanists.

Following the model of CIAM, they decided to hold a series of congresses, or concept-focused meetings where the group could collectively debate exactly how each scale of city-making should be redirected. With the Congress for the New Urbanism formally established, Duany and Plater-Zyberk led the organization of the first congress in 1993, focused on the neighborhood level and set inside a columned meeting hall in Alexandria, Virginia, called the Lyceum. Each of the founders invited people to participate. 

“It was really coming out of our Rolodexes. That I even said Rolodex probably gives you an idea of the time frame,” Moule says. “Instead of it being sort of a board meeting, we decided to make it a larger call to arms.”

About 200 people were invited, including planners, landscape architects, traffic engineers, civic activists, and developers. People made presentations about their experience and projects. “It started out as a very diversely disciplined group who were all working on the same kinds of issues,” Plater-Zyberk says.

The next congress, held in 1994, was organized by Moule and Polyzoides at the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles, and focused on the building block and the street. “That was quite provocative at the time, largely because Los Angeles was known for being the home of the automobile and the home of suburban sprawl,” Moule says. “It was sort of a stick-it-in-your-eye kind of conference.”

Calthorpe and Solomon organized the third congress in San Francisco in 1995, focused on the regional level, with an emphasis on their work planning transit-oriented development projects. The founders cast an even wider net for attendees, inviting participants from groups like AARP, the Urban Land Institute, the Trust for Public Land, and the Natural Resources Defense Council, as well as heads of departments of transportation, mayors, and government officials. “Unlike CIAM, which was only architects, we really wanted to bring in every last person that we thought had some kind of say in how the urban environment was created and made, so it was pretty diverse group,” Moule says. “It might have had 1,500 people. So there was momentum.”

Organized like conventional conferences, these three congresses had the typical hallmarks of presentations, panels, post-meeting dinners, and post-dinner parties. But unlike most conferences, where the event ends and everyone goes home, attendees were trying to build a movement—and set a new standard for neighborhood design and city building.

“People were doing things and coming back and talking to each other about the way they did it,” Polyzoides says. “We were constructing the theory out of experience, not constructing it out of theory.”

A charter signed, and an early win

New Urbanism’s fourth congress was held on May 4, 1996, in a rented hall in Charleston. The concepts and ideas generated through the previous three annual gatherings had been consolidated down into 27 principles, each roughly 25 to 50 words, and broken into three categories:

  • The metropolis, city, and town
  • The neighborhood, the district, and the corridor
  • The block, the street, and the building. 

The charter, written primarily by the founders, was presented to the invited audience. With a large white paper mounted on an easel in the center of the stage, the attendees were invited to add their signatures to adopt the charter. Though there are no records of how many people were in attendance that day, 262 signed the charter and New Urbanism became an official movement.

“It was signed dramatically. Everybody walked up on stage to sign it,” Plater-Zyberk says.

The charter signing was considered a starting point for New Urbanism, and an opening of the invitation-only organization to a broader membership. And with so much of the American landscape dominated by disconnected concentrations of single family homes or office parks or big box retail clusters, people were ready to get behind an alternative. 

By the end of 1996, CNU would claim more than 500 official members. Attendance numbers would rise with each annual congress, as did interest in the organization’s anti-sprawl sentiment. The organization’s openness and its challenges to the status quo brought attention that grew into a movement.

“We do not protect the ideas or even the use of the term New Urbanism. It’s totally freeware,” Duany says. “You can’t just get a Harvard degree. You can’t just get LEED [Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design] certification. Well, we say these are the principles called New Urbanism, don’t mangle it and get on with it.”

Sounds straightforward, but the principles called for a widespread rethinking of the accepted practices of the day, and systemic changes in the financial infrastructure of real estate development. “Segregated land use was something that was so baked into the system. You had to change how appraisals were done. You had to change how banks lent on buildings,” Moule says. “They wouldn’t lend you something if you wanted to put retail on the ground floor and housing or offices on top. It just didn’t happen.”

Some were skeptical of New Urbanism from the start. Writing in Harvard Design Magazine in 1997, the urban geographer and Marxist scholar David Harvey called out the movement as naive, arguing that it “connects to a facile contemporary attempt to transform large and teeming cities, so seemingly out of control, into an interlinked series of ‘urban villages’ where, it is believed, everyone can relate in a civil and urbane fashion to everyone else.” The head of Harvard’s Department of Urban Planning and Design in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Alex Krieger, was another critic of the movement and its emphasis on designing new communities with traditional styles instead of fixing the communities that already existed.

Not long after its official birth, New Urbanism got the chance to do just that. The HUD secretary Henry Cisneros, the highest profile signatory of the Charter of the New Urbanism, ended up enabling one of the movement’s biggest successes through the HOPE VI program. This was a HUD effort that launched in 1992 to undertake a large-scale redevelopment and revitalization of the country’s public housing projects. Throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s, CNU members and the nonprofit CNU organization itself worked directly with HUD to establish the design guidelines for the program, transforming decaying public housing barracks and towers into mixed-income neighborhoods.

The work spread across more than 260 sites in cities like Atlanta, Boston, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh, San Francisco, Charlotte, North Carolina, and Washington, D.C., and resulted in the redesign of 100,000 units of public housing. Decaying housing towers and bleak low-rise housing clusters were replaced with walkable neighborhoods that blended into their context and erased the line between public housing and the rest of the city. “Most of the members of the early CNU were very involved,” says Calthorpe. “That was really the beauty of the thing. Unlike the architects who are constantly competing with each other, we just wanted to collaborate.”

Research led by Harvard University’s Raj Chetty and released in 2026 found that children growing up in the neighborhoods revitalized through the HOPE VI program earned more money as adults, were more likely to attend college, and were less likely to be incarcerated.

“HOPE VI made policy of the idea that the design of community can have a profound influence on people’s lives,” says Mallory Baches, the current president of CNU. “It takes 30 years to do a longitudinal study on the effects of those projects, but 30 years later we have the evidence that that early influence made a big difference.”

Edging into the mainstream

Over time, many of the main principles of New Urbanism have steadily moved from the fringe of city planning and development to the mainstream. Mixed use and higher density development, and the zoning reform they tended to require, have become commonplace policies in cities across the U.S. Walkable town centers, infill development, alternative transportation, an emphasis on local economies, form-based codes, and transit-oriented development are all normal elements of many cities and their approach to growth and development. (The movement has even spawned a partly serious progressive urbanist online community called New Urbanist Memes for Transit-Oriented Teens.)

“There’s been enormous success,” says Polyzoides. “It is impossible to imagine that in a continental country like ours, you could move within a generation from people doing crap everywhere to doing the right thing on so many fronts when it comes to urbanism.”

New Urbanism and the CNU continue to affect city planning, urban development, policy, and governance, but the movement hasn’t risen to CIAM’s level of modernist influence on the shape and form of the built environment, nor has it thoroughly changed de facto development industry practices.

“New Urbanism has had a big effect, but there’s still the large companies that are buying land to build a single unit-type subdivision in the old-fashioned way,” says Plater-Zyberk. “And there’s too much of that going on. But under the current affordability crisis, in some cases, people are trying to make more of that happen.”

Calthorpe argues New Urbanism is essentially a progressive movement, with roots in the counterculture of the 1960s, and its modest uptake in the planning and development world has a lot to do with the politics of the current era. “In the end, sprawl just kept happening and we were more of a footnote or counterpoint. We never became normative in America,” he says.

One challenge that’s dogged the movement is its aesthetic lean. Style has always been a lightning rod within New Urbanism, with some embracing the movement’s goals but balking at its tendency toward classical or neotraditional architectural approaches. Plater-Zyberk recalls the issue of style being one of the biggest points of contention ahead of the charter signing back in 1996. “That was a very sensitive point,” she says. 

This aesthetic approach has recently taken on political undertones, as President Donald Trump has controversially made traditional architecture the preferred style for federal buildings.

Polyzoides, who is dean of one of the most traditionally-focused American architecture schools, rejects any connection between New Urbanism and Trump’s architectural choices, calling them an aberration. “What ties this particular president to the Mussolinis and the others in the world is they see classical architecture as an opportunity to exert power. But what classical architecture is about at its source is an architecture of community,” he says. “It’s an architecture of common expression, common ideals. So, an architecture of democracy.”

The future of the New Urbanism movement may hinge on larger concerns, and on bringing younger people into the fold. Baches, who now leads the organization, says she’s focused on helping younger generations engage with the principles and ideals set out by the founding generation of New Urbanists, many now at the tail end of their careers.

In 2023, CNU initiated a process of amending the original Charter of the New Urbanism. The amended charter now includes principles around increasing diversity, equity, and inclusion; countering involuntary displacement; ensuring the attainability of housing; and contextualizing the built environment’s role in climate change. These new principles, she argues, will keep the movement relevant into the future, while also making the output of New Urbanism—a better alternative to sprawl—even more attractive.

“Communities across the country have so much more of an appetite for great urbanism, but there’s a limited supply. And until we have created more, or adapted sprawl into better urbanism, the attainability of living the kind of quality life that great urbanism can provide is going to be only available to those who can afford it,” she says. “We need to expand access to that great urbanism.”

CNU’s 35th congress will take place in June.

#10644. Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly

As we near the launch of Motorola’s return to the flagship space, it’s becoming clear that the company is ready to fill a gap left by the departure of OnePlus, though there’s one very obvious difference between the two.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The Motorola Signature 27’s launch is coming up fast and, with it, the first truly exciting flagship the company has launched widely in quite some time. There have been a handful of high-end Moto devices in recent years, but this is the first one in quite a while where it seems Motorola is holding nothing back.

Between a powerful Snapdragon chip, top-tier cameras, and rumors of a massive battery, this is shaping up to be something special. Of course, all-out flagships like this aren’t uncommon in some parts of the world. Oppo, Honor, and other Chinese brands have been building devices like this for years but, especially in the US, they’re just completely lacking, especially now that OnePlus is dead. While OnePlus flagships in more recent years have not quite risen to the same bar as Oppo’s, they’ve been the best equivalent in the States and, now, they’re just gone.

Motorola is stepping up in a big way here, and seems to be the closest many are going to get to a OnePlus replacement.

It’s fitting, really. As much as I’d love to have Google Pixel step up its game here, Motorola’s Lenovo backing and long history in the smartphone space more than earns its spot as a proper flagship smartphone maker. The problem, really, is just going to boil down to pricing.

OnePlus was well known for top-tier specs, of course, but it built its brand on doing so at a lower price point. Even in its final days where prices were creeping higher than ever, a OnePlus flagship was still priced equal to or less than most competitors. Motorola Signature 27 does not seem to be trying to recover that part of OnePlus’ reputation based on early pricing leaks. RAMageddon surely isn’t helping matters, but Motorola’s return to the flagship space is not going to come cheap from the sound of it.

Another sore point for Motorola is in software updates, but it’s not like OnePlus was really doing that well in that regard anyway. Things are moving in a better direction with Motorola moving up to 7-year commitments on certain devices, but there’s still room for improvement and quite the poor track record to make up for.

With the launch of Motorola Signature 27 mere weeks away, I’m personally very excited to see what the company has in store. What do you think?

You’d think that Android foldables effectively doing all of the R&D for Apple’s first foldable would prevent any major issues, but apparently that’s not enough. While the scale of the problem remains unclear, Apple’s iPhone Duo is cracking for many in the same place, suggesting there’s a manufacturing problem in play. It’s not quite an OG Galaxy Fold debacle, but it doesn’t feel far off either.

Google’s latest frontier AI model has been announced in Gemini 4 Carbon. The company says it makes major leaps forward for coding and other purposes and outranks the competition but, like Argon, it’s not immediately available.

After being announced earlier this month, we reviewed the Fitbit Edge this week and the tracker is also now on sale. While it feels like an awkward middle child between the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, owners of prior Charge trackers will likely appreciate the upgrades it brings to the table.

#10643. This new software maps out a better bike network for your city

In most cities, bike networks are rolled out in disconnected pieces. A bike lane on one street might not reach the next part of a route, so you can’t necessarily ride safely across town. A new set of software tools helps planners, bike advocates, and citizens design more complete networks, automatically filling the gaps in existing infrastructure or creating the whole thing from scratch.

Called BikeNetKit, the free, open-source software is based on eight years of research on bicycle infrastructure at Denmark’s IT University of Copenhagen.

When you type in a city name, the software pulls street data from OpenStreetMap, including a map of existing bike lanes. (Getting started requires a little technical knowledge: You have to know how to use Python, and then have to enter a few lines to install and run the algorithms.)

“Planners mostly think about the small picture—what if I add a lane here? What’s on the right side and left side? But they don’t think about the network and the whole city,” says Michael Szell, an associate professor at the IT University of Copenhagen, who led the project. “Our methods are built on network science methods that look at the city from a big picture.”

One of the tools, called GrowBikeNet, can build a network from scratch—particularly useful in the U.S., where most cities have sparse bike lanes. The algorithm creates a grid of “seed points” over a city. It connects those points to any existing bike infrastructure, drawing a new map of suggested bike routes.

“The first links that are suggested are the links where you expect the most cyclists to ride,” Szell says. Rolling it out this way would create a functional network from the outset, with strong connections already in place.

Users can upload additional data to help plan a network—for example, where traffic crashes have occurred in the past, or where people typically travel each day. The software also gives the option to plan bike lanes around schools. Another tool, called Superblockify, suggests places to add car-free neighborhoods; LinkBikeNet connects gaps in otherwise well-connected networks, while FixBikeNet tells cities which gaps are most important to fix first.

The tools don’t specify what the bike infrastructure should look like. Instead of bike lanes at the side of the road, for example, some streets could be dedicated solely to people on bikes and pedestrians. Of course, that’s the opposite of most transportation planning now, which focuses on the flow of cars. “Planning for cycling is always some kind of afterthought,” says Szell.

The BikeNetKit website includes hundreds of analyses of European cities, from growing a new bike network in Kyiv, Ukraine, to fixing gaps in Copenhagen’s network, to potential car-free neighborhoods in Berlin. To try it out yourself, the open-source code is available on GitHub.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Juicebox details come from Juicebox's public pricing, product and documentation pages, checked October 14, 2026.

Pin is built for recruiting teams that want sourcing, outreach and interview scheduling in one product, and it is trusted by 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users. SHRM found AI use in HR tasks reached 43% of organizations in 2025, up from 26% in 2024. Some comparisons call Pin a solo-recruiter tool. This one checks Pin and Juicebox against their current public pages.

Pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that automates the top of the funnel, from sourcing and outreach to interview scheduling, for solo recruiters, agencies and in-house teams. Juicebox (PeopleGPT) is an AI sourcing platform that pairs natural-language candidate search with outreach sequences, ATS and CRM integrations, and add-on AI agents. For a longer feature-by-feature breakdown, see Pin's Pin vs Juicebox comparison.

No. Pin has a one-seat Solo plan at $99 a month on annual billing, and solo recruiters and small agencies use it. But Pin's team features and pricing are built for multiple users:

Juicebox does team work too. According to its pricing page (October 2026), Growth lets you invite up to five teammates to collaborate on searches, shortlists and outreach, and Business adds hiring-manager seats, usage analytics and ATS or CRM integration. Pin's team pages describe hiring managers, sourcers and closers sharing one view of the req.

Pin says it searches 850M+ profiles across multiple sources, including North America and Europe, aggregated from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. Sequences adapt per candidate, any reply pauses the sequence, and every channel stays in one thread.
