#10640. How Zohran Mamdani is convincing New York’s capitalists to give a little socialism a chance

Zohran Mamdani has not, it turns out, attempted to seize the means of production. At least not yet.

During his mayoral campaign, you couldn’t throw a stone without hitting a CEO worried about the effect he’d have on the city’s economy. After his first year in office, business is proceeding as usual, which—New Yorkers being New Yorkers—means that everyone is feeling angsty.

“I was very concerned when he was elected,” says Neil Blumenthal, cofounder and co-CEO of the nearly $3 billion eyewear company Warby Parker, headquartered in New York. Now Blumenthal is waiting to see what the most senior member of the Democratic Socialists of America in the city, if not the country, will do.

“The DSA’s official policies . . . include things like government takeover of private companies, increasing income taxes, and abolishing the police. Publicly, he’s said some things to moderate those positions,” Blumenthal says. “[But] at times he’s advocating for some of those policies, which are deeply unpopular and aren’t going to lead to growth and prosperity.”

Still, 15 chief executives have kept open enough minds to join the mayor’s Business Advisory Council. The group represents more than 100,000 employees in industries spanning real estate, film, sports, and healthcare.

It includes Hamdi Ulukaya, the billionaire CEO of Chobani, who advocates for immigrants and once played street soccer with the mayor. It also includes numerous doubters and former naysayers. There’s the real estate CEO who gave $250,000 to Mamdani’s mayoral opponent, Andrew Cuomo. The investor who wrote an op-ed saying that Mamdani would bankrupt the city. The former bank CEO who talks on Fox News about “prioritizing capitalism.” The chair of the finance committee of a hospital where Mamdani supported striking workers.

Mamdani is bringing startup culture to government

These titans of industry may not support every facet of the mayor’s ambitious plans, but they’ve signed on to his broad vision of building a better functioning, more affordable New York. Their first meeting, in September, kicked off with an icebreaker about their first jobs, and they discussed a key point of alignment with the mayor’s agenda: The high cost of housing and childcare is making it difficult to hire in New York. (Neither Mamdani nor the council members agreed to be interviewed for this story, though top administration figures happily did.)

“I’ve seen this TV series for a lot of episodes,” says Anthony Shorris, head of the New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC), the city’s primary economic development vehicle. Shorris has worked alongside business leaders, often as a public servant, since the 1980s. “They love mayors, they get mad at mayors, whatever. At the end of the day, I think what they really care about is the city’s economy being strong.”

Mamdani has brought an undeniable sense of energy and optimism to the job, which had “been missing for quite a while,” says Shorris.

He’s also brought some much-needed elements of startup culture to city government. That includes quick response times, vibrant interactive marketing campaigns, improved city websites, and hands-on servant leadership. He tackled certain small—sometimes symbolic—things right away, such as filling potholes quickly (the city has fixed more than 200,000 so far in 2026, more than it did the entire year prior, under Eric Adams), replacing nets in basketball hoops, offering free opera tickets, creating public viewings for World Cup and Knicks playoff games, providing evening childcare for parents who need a night out, and installing modular public bathrooms.

It’s part of a larger plan. When constituents “feel a greater sense of confidence in government, that gives us more room to tackle even bigger things that people in the past have not thought of as the fundamental basic role of government,” says Julie Su, in the newly titled position of deputy mayor for economic justice.

Even skeptical business leaders can see that Mamdani currently enjoys an eye-popping 69% approval rating. All five of the ballot initiatives he championed——like speeding up bike lane projects and construction—passed handily.

In the aftermath of a generational wave of Democratic victories at every level of government across every part of the country during the midterms (including eight DSA members elected to Congress), it’s hard to generalize about what, exactly, individual voters were responding to. But Mamdani’s relentless focus on affordability was echoed by politicians across the Democratic Party.

And fear that Mamdani’s vocal support of democratic socialism would haunt Democrats was certainly misplaced. Earlier in the year, House Speaker Mike Johnson threatened to make him the face of the national Democratic Party in order to drag down Democratic chances in Middle America. Today, aligning with Mamdani is a PR win, though some leaders will keep queuing up “mad at mayor” episodes no matter what.

But as Mamdani moves past these early victories and begins tackling his more ambitious agenda, the détente that’s existed with the business community since his inauguration is starting to be tested.

His to-do list is long and only fractionally complete: city-owned grocery stores, free childcare for 2-year-olds, faster buses (with a plan to make them free, which would require state-government support), expanded access to union organizing, rent freezes for one- and two-year leases (roughly 1 million units total, about 40% of the city’s rental units), a pathway for citizens to sue businesses or landlords they feel are breaking the law, zoning rules that make it easier to build new (and more affordable) apartments, fewer hurdles and fines around small business operation, and the enforcement of city laws, like winning a recent $131.5 million action against DoorDash for underpaying delivery workers.

And then there are his even grander plans, some of which have a more quintessentially “eat the rich” bent: a “pied-à-terre tax” on expensive second homes in the city (that remains tangled in legal challenges), increased minimum wage, and higher taxes on the wealthy and corporations—all of which require support from a state government less aligned with his vision.

What the city’s CEOs really think about their mayor

The business impact of Mamdani’s agenda won’t be measured in immediate increases to market cap or earnings per share. It will be felt obliquely. Corporations benefit when employees can access affordable housing and childcare and customers have disposable income to purchase their products.

America’s captains of industry know this. Despite the rending of garments before the election last year about New York turning into Soviet Russia, many of them took similar positions not long ago.

The Business Roundtable, comprising some of the largest corporations in America, issued passionate statements in 2019 about the value of stakeholder capitalism, the same year that Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan touted large wage increases for workers and Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff proclaimed that “capitalism as we know it is dead.” Recently, CEO Scott Kirby of United Airlines told The New York Times that “wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that. We should have a national wealth tax.”

After the midterms, other leaders began giving voice to such values. Appearing on CNBC the day after the election, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi noted: “If you look over the past 20 years, return on capital has increased very, very significantly. You can’t say the same thing about return on labor.” (Continues…)

To pursue his daring agenda, Mamdani has put some ballast in place. In addition to deputy mayor Su, who led the U.S. Department of Labor as acting secretary for two years under President Biden, Mamdani brought on Shorris, a former first deputy mayor under Bill de Blasio and Port Authority executive director, to be the president and CEO of the NYCEDC.

He’s paired with new NYCEDC board chair Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair known for finding ways businesses were crushing regular people and regulating them out of existence, making her a bugbear of corporate interests. Khan tells me via email that she’s focused on wielding the NYCEDC’s toolkit to grow “the economy in a way that delivers affordability, widespread prosperity, and real opportunity.”

The next three years—or seven, should Mamdani be reelected—could end up being nothing but a tense standoff. Or they could usher in the most progressive economic intervention since the New Deal. I spoke with members of the administration, business leaders, political insiders, and policy experts carrying out parts of his agenda to answer a fundamental question of his first term: whether the democratic socialism that propelled Mamdani to victory can coexist with the capitalist engine powering the financial heart of America.

Democratic socialism and its deep-pocketed foes

What does it mean, in practice, for Mamdani to be a democratic socialist? It’s tricky: Ask two socialists to define socialism and you’ll get five answers.

Mamdani gave his most digestible definition in October to podcaster Theo Von: “Socialism means you will have whatever you need to live a dignified life—and that it is the government’s job to deliver on that.”

For many, the sentiment has become a rallying cry. Since he became mayor, DSA membership has grown to more than 120,000 nationwide—the New York chapter now includes 15,000 members, more than the entire national organization had in 2016. (Full disclosure: I’m a former member of the San Francisco chapter of DSA and a former union organizer. I’ve also been a business editor for more than a decade—a living embodiment of the tension I’m writing about here.)

Mamdani has tapped into a sense that socialism “really cares about excellence,” says Corey Robin, a political science professor at Brooklyn College. His vision “gives people a hint of the kinds of things that the government can provide to make life better, not as a default for what the private sector doesn’t provide, but perhaps as a baseline of what we can all expect for everybody.”

If the opposition to Mamdani’s movement has a spiritual home base, it might be outside Citadel CEO Ken Griffin’s 24,000-square-foot four-floor penthouse on the southern edge of New York’s Central Park.

To announce the pied-à-terre tax—which would tax second homes in New York valued by the city as $5 million or more for houses and $1 million or more for condos and co-ops (at rates between 0.8% and 6.5%)—the mayor released a video of himself standing in front of the hedge fund leader’s second home and crowing about the tax dollars Griffin would soon be paying. The tax, Mamdani said, was “designed for the richest of the rich: those who store their wealth in New York City real estate but don’t actually live here.” The video’s soundtrack sounded remarkably similar to the theme song from HBO’s Succession.

For some in the upper echelons of industry, it was a bridge too far. “New York City is the financial home of the world, and to have a mayor that truly believes that capitalism and jobs are evil . . . publicly humiliating Ken Griffin and actively trying to drive [him] away is a pretty terrible outcome for the day-to-day New Yorkers who need jobs,” says Bradley Tusk, a venture capitalist and political consultant who worked in Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s administration. “More tax revenue means you can help more poor people. . . . Instead, he is actively pushing people away.”

Mamdani “was playing to his base and sending a negative message,” says James Whelan, president of the Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY), a trade group that represents some 14,000 members. “We want people to invest here in the city, create jobs here. There was no upside to that video in terms of what was in the city’s best interest.”

Hedge fund manager Bill Ackman called the video “a huge mistake” at Fast Company’s Innovation Festival in September. He admonished the mayor for having “scared away or encouraged people who are among the most productive New Yorkers to go to other places, like Miami.”

Griffin himself claimed that the video “put me in harm’s way” and threatened to halt plans to build a new Citadel headquarters in Midtown.

Compared to the rhetoric coming out of D.C., Mamdani’s video seems tame—and comes nowhere near the language that, say, FDR used when talking about the “economic royalists” of his era, according to Robin, the Brooklyn College professor. Yet there’s still the question of the mayor’s other tax proposals.

During the campaign, Mamdani teased a slate of increases: raising the income tax by 2% on people earning more than $1 million (projected to raise $4 billion annually), adjusting property taxes so wealthier property owners pay more, and raising the state’s corporate tax rate on some businesses from 7.25% to 11.5% to match neighboring New Jersey’s (projected to raise $5 billion a year).

But only the state legislature and Governor Kathy Hochul can raise these taxes. And while she supported the pied-à-terre tax, Hochul seems currently uninterested in signing any other large tax proposals. (On Election Day, when asked if he had spoken to the governor about new tax proposals during her next term, Mamdani sidestepped the question).

In some ways, it’s all a bit of theater. The mayor can energize supporters by calling for a tax he can’t raise. CEOs can wring hands about the possibility of a tax that will not be enacted. But business leaders hate uncertainty, so “words matter,” says Blumenthal. “If we are trying to make New York City the best place to build a business, and you are telling folks, ‘Hey, we’re going to be raising taxes’ or are generally promoting an anti-business sentiment, those business leaders have lots of options” in terms of moving to other cities, he warns.

“It’s cordial.”

While evidence of people and businesses fleeing the city will take years to quantify, initial numbers don’t scream of any danger. Available office space just fell to its lowest level since 2020, and in the second quarter, contracts on $10 million to $20 million properties were up nearly 40% over the same period last year.

Despite Griffin’s protests, he’s continuing his Midtown office project. Ackman announced plans to open a $660 million brain research institute on the city’s West Side. Higher corporate tax rates could certainly drive businesses away, or suppress entrepreneurship, but Mamdani’s proposal was aimed at the highest-earning companies; a new startup would be exempt.

Is Warby Parker toying with the idea of leaving? “We’re a New York brand, so we’re here, and we’re going to do everything possible to continue to invest in this city,” Blumenthal says, citing the company’s continued charitable commitment to give free glasses to New York schoolchildren.

Everybody’s Business: When it comes to his economic vision for New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is surrounded by supporters and detractors. Yet everyone’s got to find a way to work together, at least for the next three years. A look at who’s who among this smart, engaged, and very motley crew.

[carousel_block id=”carousel-1793990648969″]

Some of the tension seems entirely avoidable. Business leaders, used to knowing what levers to pull and what phone call to make, are having trouble getting used to an administration that isn’t as focused on the usual glad-handing. “He’s so charismatic that if he was willing to spend a little bit of time meeting with VCs, with startups, he could make them feel good about being here,” says Tusk.

“Many in the business community, myself included, would love to see a more pro-business approach,” says Julie Samuels, the president and CEO of Tech:NYC, a trade group that represents the city’s tech industry. Even so, she acknowledges, the administration is making an effort: “There is outreach.”

It helps that the city’s vibes have been good. The Knicks’ championship run, which prompted a jaded populace to party in the streets, coupled with the mayor’s constant barrage of smiling, feel-good videos about small wins (another pothole filled!) have created a sense of possibility. “As long as New York is a place where people want to live, tech companies will continue to expand and hire here,” says Samuels. Plus, “this administration is, especially at an interpersonal level, very pleasant. That goes a long way for those of us who work in this space.”

(“It’s good that we communicate,” says Steven Fulop, the president and CEO of the nonprofit Partnership for New York City, which represents more than 300 of the city’s largest corporations, who is often deeply critical of the administration. “It’s cordial.”)

“There’s certainly common ground, and that’s not always reported,” deputy mayor Su says. A big part of her job involves meeting with CEOs—and sometimes cleaning up. She happened to have a meeting scheduled with Whelan the day after the Griffin video dropped. “It went fine,” says Whelan.

Su cites the Business Advisory Council as evidence of the administration’s willingness to engage with some of its biggest critics: “This is not a performative exercise” but “a real desire to learn from one another.” Those don’t sound like the words of an administration that’s trying to end private capital. But that doesn’t mean another video targeting the 1% is off the table.

Mamdani’s grocery plan: “I think it’s incredibly stupid, but it’s at least a real attempt at socialism”

Errol Schweizer remembers being shocked when he saw the video. In December 2024, Mamdani, then a long-shot candidate running for mayor of New York, promised that if he won, he’d open city-owned grocery stores. There were scant details about how this might work, but it sounded like a revolutionary idea.

“He pulled it out of his ass,” jokes Schweizer, a consultant and former food executive who hosts the Grocery Nerds podcast. “There was nothing else to it. He was like, ‘We’re going to open five publicly owned grocery stores.’” For Schweizer, though, it resonated. A former vice president of the grocery division of Whole Foods, he has been writing about the logistics of city-owned groceries for years.

Schweizer eventually got in touch with the campaign and, after Mamdani’s election, helped the NYCEDC design the city’s $70 million pilot program. The five outposts, the first of which is slated to open by late 2027, will be spread across the five boroughs and be run by private operators. The administration says they’ll charge 30% less on average than nearby stores on all fresh produce, meat, seafood, and roughly 20 additional categories of pantry staples, dairy, and refrigerated goods.

Of all the administration’s projects, the grocery stores are the most forward- looking and traditionally “socialist.” They’ve also drawn the most criticism. The grocery business has infamously tight margins, and since the plan is for the city to make payments to the store operator to compensate for its losses, critics say the stores will cost the city too much to subsidize. Even many left-leaning wonks say there are simpler alternatives to lowering the price of food for needy New Yorkers, like increasing payments to existing food-subsidy programs.

Schweizer says the existence of other options misses the point. By controlling the grocery stores, the city gets to play a role in the supply chain. If the cost of food is adding to the city’s affordability crisis, the administration doesn’t want to let private operators or other market forces exclusively determine that cost. “New York does a lot of this stuff already in other sectors,” says Schweizer. Its ferry system, for instance, is publicly owned but outsourced to private operators. In this case, public institutions become “a primary purchaser of food for customers,” he says.

As one of the most radical of the administration’s proposals, the stores have become a lightning rod. “I think it’s incredibly stupid, but it’s at least a real attempt at socialism,” says Tusk. A coalition of small grocery stores and the National Supermarket Association have both sued the city, saying the plan is illegally anti-competition. In response to the proposal, John Catsimatidis, the billionaire owner and CEO of supermarket chain Gristedes, threatened to close his stores if Mamdani won the election. (He is also a former Republican mayoral candidate and the owner of a right-wing radio station, so he may not be motivated strictly by the bottom line.)

Schweizer acknowledges that the stores will have an impact on surrounding businesses, which the city will need to mitigate, perhaps with additional subsidies. But he sees an upside for the city’s economy: “There are 1.5 million New Yorkers who are food insecure.” And they spend money too. “That is an enormous customer base that’s not being serviced by the current market. It’s a market failure.”

In a few years, there will be data—and it won’t require much complex analysis. “The measure of success here is, will people shop?” says Schweizer.

It’s just one example of how the city may intervene in the local economy. One of the next “failed markets” the city is looking at fixing, Shorris says, is building insurance, which drives up the cost of housing development. Additional new initiatives could address “monopolistic practices or limited suppliers,” he says. “We want to look at the range of tools we have—regulatory, policymaking, use of our land and resources, investment, and scale—to see if we can create opportunities that the market might not [be creating] for the people we’re concerned about.”

The symbolism of toilets

“Everyone would tell us, ‘Oh man, New York City, it’ll take, minimum, a year and a half to get something through the procurement process, and that’s going to be a slog,’” says Jessica Heinzelman. As the cofounder and COO of Throne Labs, which has installed modular restrooms in six U.S. markets, she had been eyeing New York for years but thought the red tape would be daunting.

Then free public toilets appeared on the mayor’s agenda for his first 100 days. Five weeks after the inauguration, a request went out for proposals, and Throne—which sells toilet stalls that operate on a 10-minute timer and don’t require water lines or electricity hookups—won. By September 16, Throne was installing the first of what will be 17 units as part of a one-year, $4 million pilot. (Heinzelman says OSHA rules prevented the mayor from helping install a toilet himself at the launch event. When she suggested they stage it, she was told Mamdani won’t do anything fake.)

This is not the speed at which cities usually move—even one that never sleeps. The mayor, says Shorris, “is impatient” and devotes a lot of attention to the “key areas that were commitments of his.” The business world is noticing. “Obviously, what they’re doing and saying is resonating with a lot of New Yorkers,” says Samuels, of Tech:NYC. “And a lot of people in tech, particularly on the investor side, see that and want to know what’s going on. What is it that’s resonating?”

Take, for example, the city’s Parents’ Night Out babysitting project. One Sunday in August, rec centers around the city opened from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. for children ages 6 to 13, providing free activities and childcare for up to nearly 300 registered children. In a city of 8 million, 300 sets of parents getting four hours off is an almost meaningless statistic. But that a government would even think of it is the point.

That may have been a one-off event, but childcare is a top issue for the administration, and an area where it’s forging some of its most productive relationships with business leaders.

With a year of childcare now costing sometimes even more than a year of college, the mayor worked with the governor to launch a pilot expanding former mayor de Blasio’s universal 3-K program—which in 2017 seemed revolutionary but is now part of the city fabric—to 2-year-olds, up to 10 hours a day, 260 days a year. Initially, the program will serve roughly 2,000 children, with plans to expand to 12,000 by fall 2027. After that, it becomes a question of how to pay for more, with business leaders likely to balk at raising taxes.

What’s interesting is that everyone—even business leaders put off by the mayor’s socialism—seems to agree that childcare should be free, a public good provided by the city.

In September, a group of businesses—including the Partnership for New York City, Tech:NYC, and REBNY—established the NYC Child Care Business Council to advocate for public investment in childcare. “The market is not able to solve this problem,” says Grace Rauh, executive director of Citizens Union, which is home to the 5BORO Institute, a New York policy think tank that convened the group. “Frankly, private businesses aren’t able to provide the kind of fully robust childcare benefits that their employees need.” But they increasingly recognize, she says, that for the city’s economy to grow and for it to attract the best talent, “we need affordable and accessible childcare.”

Mamdani’s real estate turnaround

Not everyone is satisfied with the administration’s overall pace of change. Andrew Rigie, executive director of the New York City Hospitality Alliance, which represents restaurants, bars, and clubs, feels that Mamdani’s OPEN for Small Business initiative—more than 50 proposals for eliminating red tape and fines—doesn’t go far enough. “While none of them are bad,” he says, “they’re certainly not transformative.”

But even some of Mamdani’s fiercest critics are realizing the benefits of a city that makes things happen. Two months before the mayoral election, an email circulated among housing developers, the Times reported: “If we fail to mobilize, the financial capital of the world risks being handed over to a socialist this November. We cannot—and will not—let that happen.”

But Mamdani, who once advocated for “moving toward the full de-commodification of housing,” came around over the next several months to the potential of private real estate development, citing building booms in Austin and Minneapolis that seemed to lower rents. The Economist declared in September, nine months into his administration, that “developers are learning to love Zohran Mamdani.” REBNY’s Whelan confirms it (while also decrying the rent freeze and Mamdani’s “punitive” attitude toward building owners): “When it comes to the issue of housing production, our goals are aligned,” he tells me. “We have a housing-supply issue here in New York City. The mayor has ambitious goals, and he should. Now it’s a matter of whether execution will meet ambition.”

The real estate industry certainly supports Mamdani’s effort to speed up permits and building approvals and his goal to increase supply by 200,000 new affordable apartments over the next decade. That’s a lot of new business for developers. “Real estate is an asset class that can’t move” out of the city, says Whelan. “So it’s in our interest for the city to succeed. If this mayor makes progress in making the city more affordable, creating more housing, we’re going to be a more competitive city, and the real estate industry is going to be stronger.”

Mamdani has even seemingly charmed New York’s most legendary real estate developer, receiving gushing praise from President Trump at joint appearances in recent months despite the president’s once calling him a “100% Communist Lunatic.”

Trump has also given him a template for one of his biggest moves since he took office: having the NYCEDC invest $29 million into the building of a quantum lab at New York University. In return, the city will take 15% of any future revenue from the IP generated on city-funded equipment. A few years ago, this would have seemed like a radical socialist endeavor. But given that the president has spent the past two years negotiating equity stakes for the federal government in major tech and mineral companies (including a nearly 10% stake in Intel), this deal feels positively quaint as an act of government intervention.

The quantum computing arrangement is a prime example of how the NYCEDC will be thinking about its bigger economic development projects. “This mayor’s made pretty clear what his priority is, which is to find opportunities for growth that advance the objective of social justice,” Shorris says. Some projects will be solely about creating jobs, and others—like the grocery stores—will be focused on improving economic opportunity. But the ideal one will sit in the middle. “I don’t think the growth and justice objectives are incompatible,” Shorris says.

Good vibes, it turns out, are good for business

Since Mamdani’s electrifying mayoral run, politicians across the country have tried to emulate his video strategy, with limited success (just ask Mayor Karen Bass in Los Angeles, whose own pothole video failed to land). They’re having better luck on the policy front: delivering key services while gently prying the capitalist system open to greater government control.

In Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu is clashing with business interests over tax increases and development, while testing programs like free buses. She crushed her most recent primary challenger, the son of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, by 49 points.

In L.A., city council member and DSA-endorsee Nithya Raman, running for mayor on a strikingly Mamdani-esque platform of improving city services and increasing housing development while focusing on the city’s lower-income residents, defeated Bass, the incumbent—while Washington, D.C. and Providence, Rhode Island, also elected new socialist mayors.

(On the other hand, Brandon Johnson, the Chicago mayor whose own grocery pilot failed, and Katie Wilson, the recently elected socialist mayor of Seattle, are floundering, hinting that ideology must be paired with execution to fully inspire.)

A quarter of the way into his term, Mamdani has yet to be tested by a crisis or severe economic downturn. The AI bubble could pop, the bond market is creaky, and tensions between him and his base about policing—and the continued employment of Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch—could crest. (Retaining Tisch from the previous administration was universally cited by business leaders I spoke with as the best decision he’s made, making her seem like a foundational piece of any bridges being built.)

Meanwhile, in order to enact some of his most progressive proposals, he’ll have to persuade state-level lawmakers to support and pay for them—and face down corporate leaders. “He hasn’t yet had the kinds of confrontations with private capital that are going to have to happen for some of these big changes to happen,” says Robin, the Brooklyn College professor. But political capital is currency: A near-70% approval rating means you have room to try things.

“There’s tremendous power inside government agencies that has not been fully utilized for the good of the many, to build an economy for the many,” says deputy mayor Su. If more politicians figure out how to unleash it, the movement could gain even more traction—in New York and elsewhere.

By doing things like cutting red tape for small business and appointing chief savings officers to eliminate wasteful spending in city departments, while also pushing city-owned grocery stores and universal childcare, perhaps the mayor has replaced the usual binary of “more government” or “less government” with a new paradigm: Can we find the right amount of government to solve each problem?

Industry leaders can help answer that question. Billionaires, industry groups, and corporate lobbying arms spent tens of millions of dollars trying to prevent Mamdani from being elected. Now, they’re trying to figure out their place in a city where his agenda (or, at least, his presentation of his agenda) has become quite popular. Good vibes, it turns out, are good for business. So are functioning cities, and employees who aren’t struggling to afford housing, childcare, and groceries. Mamdani’s success could end up saving capitalism in New York from the die-hard capitalists themselves.

Wary business leaders have a list of indicators they’re watching to determine the administration’s success. Have jobs left the city? Is the number of millionaires increasing? Is new housing being built? “Does New York become a better place to build a business, raise a family, and invest for the future?” offers Blumenthal, citing New York’s shrinking population. “Is homelessness down? Are reading scores significantly better? Are the streets safer and cleaner?”

Shorris says the vision is to hit those metrics. “A New York that spreads its benefits across all of its people has been and can continue to be the most powerful economic engine anywhere,” he says. There’s a place at the table for business leaders to help build that city under a democratic socialist administration. They’re just going to have to get used to the fact that they’re no longer the ones controlling the agenda.

#10637. These Soviet anti-drinking PSAs show a different side of Russian propaganda

In the final years of Soviet Union, the government tried curbing drinking with public service announcements that visualized alcohol as death. A new exhibition called Just Say Nyet collects the best of them from the late 1980s that looks a little different than what you might first think of when it comes to Soviet propaganda.

Curated by B.A. Van Sise, the exhibition runs from November 12 to April 11, 2027 at Poster House in New York City. This work shows a visual style distinct from the early-20th century Russian constructivist style of big, bold, blocky typography paired with grids and diagonals, or socialist realism, a style associated with mid-20th century Soviet propaganda showing images of people working together in solidarity or depicting the work of the individual as for the good of the whole.

The look of Soviet public health PSAs in the 1980s involves simple symbols like alcohol bottles and labels that are centered in the messaging. The idea is to make visual metaphors about why drinking is deadly as minimal and easy to understand as possible.

“It echoes, in many ways, all the other efforts happening in the waning days of the Soviet Union,” Van Sise tells Fast Company, which he describes as a “humanist view of the problem,” for lack of a better term, because it “focused more on individual health and wealth rather than a person’s value to the state.”

This more humanist approach to government propaganda can also been seen in other antidrug and morality PSAs of the ’80s.

“What’s different here is that you see the concept move from stick to carrot,” Van Sise says.

The work doesn’t depict alcoholism as a drag on the wider society; it asks viewers to consider why quitting drinking is better for them. The message is individualistic, not collectivist. The artist behind one poster called “Don’t Lose Face” replaced a young person’s face with an alcohol bottle as a warning that drinking could cost them their personal identity.

The exhibition also includes work like “Alcohol Destroys Life,” a 1989 poster that shows a bottle crushing a man, and “Lethally Harmful” from the same year, depicting a bottle shape inside a razor blade cutting into a heart shape. The message is that alcohol kills.

“Physical Education is Health! That’s the Only Way!” from 1988 shows a soccer ball smashing a bottle of vodka, while “Alcohol is the Enemy of Life,” by the designers Sergei Bulkin and Evgeniya Mikheeva, the team that also designed the razor blade and heart poster, uses the label from a bottle as a sheet draped over a dead body on an autopsy table.

The Soviet government launched the anti-drinking campaign in May 1985 as the most serious state-sanctioned effort to curb alcoholism since prohibition during World War I. The truth was, the country had a long-running drinking problem.

By 1986, per capita alcohol consumption in the USSR had doubled over 30 years, the CIA estimated at the time. The agency blamed rising alcoholism there on factors like societal stresses and a low quality of life, and said it contributed to problems like industrial accidents, worker absenteeism, violent crimes, and declining life expectancy.

By 1985, the Soviet government enacted stricter rules around alcohol consumption and sale, and cut back on state production of alcohol while launching the PSA campaign. The campaign ultimately wasn’t successful, however. It failed for the same reason the U.S. ended Prohibition during the Great Depression and a French sobriety campaign in the 1950s and ’60s floundered: A lot of people drink to make the world hurt a little less for them, and that can’t be conquered with sloganeering.

“People like a drink. Some people need a drink,” Van Sise says. “Americans made liquor illegal, the French made it questionable, the Soviets made it undesirable. But at the end of the day, no slogan is going to dissuade somebody with tremors.”

#10634. Meet the California Science Center’s new gateway to STEM careers

A film about the space shuttle ends with a majestic launch and rocket exhaust filling the screen. Suddenly, real-life fog envelops the theater, before the walls part and the haze dissipates to reveal a gasp-inducing 200-foot Space Shuttle Endeavour, nose up, facing skyward.

This Hollywood finish—Endeavour is the only authentic space shuttle presented with fuel tank and solid rocket boosters stacked for launch—is the centerpiece of the California Science Center’s new $450 million Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, which opens November 13 after more than three decades in the making.

More than 200 aerospace artifacts and interactive exhibits fill three airy, multilevel galleries that illustrate the history and physics of flight, space exploration, and autonomous craft. But it’s the spectacle of Endeavour that symbolizes the CSC’s mission as Southern California’s gateway drug to science. The air and space wing comes at a time when the state’s $366 billion space technology sector is desperate for more STEM talent in a region often regarded as the epicenter of the space startup economy.

“We want to be a feeder into all kinds of science, engineering, and STEM careers,” Jeffrey Rudolph, the CSC president and CEO, tells Fast Company. “Getting particularly young people, who may not have thought of themselves as belonging in science and engineering, interested and involved. Even if they don’t want to go into science, we think it’s good to have a basic understanding of it.”

“There’s a war on science going on in our country right now,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said during a press preview last month. “That has implications not just for air and space, but for healthcare, all kinds of decisions. We want to help change that. This is a physical manifestation of what California values.”

The CSC’s mandate includes reducing initial barriers to science and guiding STEM career aspirants to their next steps. Beyond free admission, CSC offers a summer science camp, professional development for science educators, and high school internships that expose students to local aerospace companies and institutions.

The study of flight

The Oschin wing’s impact on science advocacy was in evidence even before its opening. In July, Astronauts for America used the shuttle as a backdrop to kick off its American college tour encouraging students to vote. Kenneth Phillips, the physicist who is CSC’s curator for aerospace science, designed the Oschin exhibits around a freshman course he teaches at the University of Southern California, even enlisting students to prototype several interactive exhibits. The opening expects some 30 astronauts, including Endeavour’s final mission crew, led by Mark Kelly, now a U.S. senator from Arizona. 

The 200,000-square-foot expansion (as big as three and a half football fields) roughly doubles the Los Angeles science center’s exhibit space, boasting a dizzying array of air and spacecraft that hang from the ceiling and jet up from lower floors. There are authentic Gemini 11 and SpaceX Dragon cargo capsules, a 3D-printed 60-foot Electron rocket from Rocket Lab, Joby eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft), a drone display, and immersive experiences like an International Space Station fly-through simulation and a flight to Seoul inside a Korean Air Boeing 747-400 cockpit. A collaboration with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology describes their planetary exploration and Earth observation work through replicas of lunar and Martian probes, snakelike exploration robots, and the opportunity to program a Mars rover mission.

The 20-story Endeavour, alongside its orange propellant container and two solid rocket boosters, holds court in the cavernous shuttle gallery. Its base lies 25 feet below, accessible in part by a dark 45-foot tunnel slide with turns that replicate the shuttle’s reentry path, an idea borrowed from Kennedy Space Center’s Atlantis shuttle showcase. (“We saw that and said, ‘That’s good, but we can make it bigger and better,'” Rudolph laughs.) Several levels offer close-up views into the cockpit and mid-deck, and a payload bay stocked with supplies; above, there’s a glass platform from which visitors can look down on the entire shuttle.

“We wanted to show the whole system in launch position to explain the science and engineering behind it and give a better understanding of the enormous amount of energy it takes to get off the surface of Earth and into orbit,” says Rudolph. “And it is the most majestic way to see it.”

These views, once reserved only for NASA engineers, astronauts, and their families, “we now get to share with the rest of the world,” says the retired NASA astronaut John “Danny” Olivas, who flew two shuttle missions and advised on the Oschin Center. “The visual experience does a much better job of capturing the enormity of it.”

We got the space shuttle. Now what?

Getting hold of a retired shuttle to display in launch position was always part of CSC’s master plan, adopted in 1993, and the center won Endeavour from NASA in 2011 in a competition among museums. (The other three shuttles—Atlantis, Enterprise, and Discovery—reside on the East Coast.) Aside from the state’s long history with the aerospace industry, the shuttles were designed, built, and often landed in California.

“So, we got it,” says Rudolph. “And then we’re like, ‘Now what?’”

CSC brass set about raising money, figuring out transportation logistics, locating or fabricating missing shuttle pieces, and designing the first building to house a vertical shuttle outside of a NASA or Air Force facility, feats requiring the guidance of NASA engineers. Funding came from its namesake, Samuel Oschin, the Los Angeles entrepreneur who died in 2003; the state of California; state-backed bonds; and private donations, which are still being raised. (Also, some exhibit elements come from commercial and institutional partnerships.) Meanwhile, they had to get Endeavour to Los Angeles, and to the center.

“We had no idea how complex it was. We probably wouldn’t have done it if we did,” says Rudolph. “A lot of the folks at NASA didn’t think we could pull off getting it from LAX to the science center, because you can’t take it apart like an airplane. We’d never be able to put it back together again.”

In 2012, the shuttle—ferried atop a modified Boeing 747 shuttle carrier aircraft—famously flew around California, over NASA facilities and iconic landmarks, before landing at Los Angeles International Airport. Then it was transported, on a specialized rolling steel platform, slowly through a 12-mile nonlinear street route that had to be more than 78 feet wide with no overhangs below 60 feet high, passing 1.5 million cheering onlookers. The tank came by barge through the Panama Canal, up the West Coast to Marina Del Rey, before moving through the streets. “Almost half a million people showed up—for a fuel tank,” says Rudolph.

After more than a decade in a horizontal stance in a CSC atrium, Endeavour was ready for its final liftoff. In early 2024, a massive 450-foot crane hoisted the shuttle by sling, turned it upright, and slowly lowered it—with an inch to spare on either side—onto an isolated concrete seismic slab on ball bearings to move with earthquakes. Given the beating it had to take from launch and reentry, “we figured that the shuttle as a design can withstand the worst earthquake anyone’s predicting for L.A.,” says Dennis Jenkins, the Oschin Center project director, who spent three decades as a NASA contractor working on the shuttles.

The Oschin Air and Space Center’s long journey to realization ends with a first step for a new generation of explorers, enthusiasts, and even creatives seeking inspiration from new frontiers. Eventually, the air and space center hopes to collaborate with the nearby Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Natural History Museum of L.A. County, and California African American Museum. 

“The country really needs science and engineering more than ever now, but it’s more than just STEM,” says Rudolph. “Space inspires across the entire spectrum of human expression.”

#10633. How to Optimize AI-Generated Images for Faster Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated images are becoming a common part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product illustrations, landing pages, blog posts, and digital interfaces. However, generating an image is only one part of the process. Before publishing it, developers need to ensure that the image loads quickly, displays correctly across devices, and maintains its visual quality.

Large image files can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay the appearance of important content. These problems can affect user experience and website performance, particularly on mobile devices and slower internet connections.

A reliable image optimization workflow helps address these challenges. By selecting appropriate dimensions, choosing efficient image formats, automating image processing, and implementing responsive delivery, developers can improve loading performance without sacrificing visual quality.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques and development tools.

Images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. Uploading large, unoptimized images can make pages slower and increase the amount of data visitors need to download.

Several common problems contribute to poor image performance:

Incorrect dimensions waste bandwidth on smaller screens.

Missing image dimensions can cause unexpected layout shifts.

Poor responsive configuration can make browsers download unnecessarily large images.

Incorrect loading priorities can delay important visual content.

These issues can affect Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

For developers, image optimization should therefore be part of the website development workflow rather than a final task performed immediately before publication.

Before optimizing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small interface graphic.

For example, a website might use the following dimensions:

These dimensions are examples rather than fixed requirements. The appropriate size depends on the website layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

When preparing source visuals, developers can explore different AI image generation options and consider how the generated images will fit their intended layouts.

Once the image is ready, keep a high-quality master file. This allows developers to create smaller versions for different screen sizes without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Avoid enlarging small images unnecessarily because upscaling can introduce blur and visible artifacts.

Choosing the right format can reduce image size while preserving acceptable visual quality.

Three commonly used formats are AVIF, WebP, and JPEG.

AVIF: Often provides efficient compression for photographs and detailed illustrations. It can significantly reduce file sizes, although encoding may take longer.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation. It offers broad browser support and is suitable for many website images.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and situations where compatibility with older software or systems is important.

PNG is appropriate for certain lossless graphics, screenshots, and images that require transparency. However, it can produce unnecessarily large files when used for photographic content.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare file sizes and inspect visual quality before selecting the final output.

A practical approach is to generate AVIF and WebP versions and provide a JPEG fallback where necessary.

Manually resizing and converting images becomes time-consuming when a website contains dozens or hundreds of visual assets.

Automation makes the process more consistent. Developers can use Sharp, a Node.js image-processing library, to resize images, convert formats, and generate multiple versions from a single source file.

Next, create a file named build-images.mjs:

The script creates multiple image sizes in both WebP and AVIF formats.

The quality settings are starting points, not universal recommendations. Developers should adjust them after checking the resulting file sizes and visual details.

This approach is particularly useful for content-heavy websites, product catalogs, and applications that publish images regularly.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on the visitor's screen and the space available in the layout.

HTML provides two important attributes for this purpose: srcset and sizes.

The srcset attribute lists the available image files and their widths. The sizes attribute describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes.

In this example, the image is expected to occupy approximately 720 pixels on wider screens and nearly the full viewport width on smaller screens.

The browser uses this information to choose an appropriate image candidate.

One common mistake is setting sizes="100vw" for an image that occupies only a small part of the page. This can encourage the browser to download a larger file than necessary.

Always ensure that the sizes attribute reflects the actual website layout.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide multiple image formats and a fallback option.

The browser selects a supported format, while the img element provides the fallback image and alternative text.

Developers should verify that every referenced file exists and that its dimensions match the intended layout.

The picture element can also support different crops for desktop and mobile devices. This is useful when a wide banner needs a separate composition for smaller screens.

Images without defined dimensions can cause content to move while the browser loads the file. This behavior contributes to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Including width and height attributes helps browsers reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

For responsive layouts, developers can use CSS:

This allows images to scale within their containers while maintaining their proportions.

Images below the initial viewport can generally use native lazy loading:

However, the main hero image should not normally be lazy-loaded when it is responsible for LCP. Delaying an important above-the-fold image can make the page appear slower.

Where appropriate, developers can use fetchpriority="high" for the main image to help the browser prioritize its download.

The correct strategy depends on the image's position and importance within the page.

Image optimization involves more than file size and dimensions. Developers should also consider accessibility, file organization, and metadata.

Alternative text helps people using screen readers understand meaningful images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page.

Decorative images that provide no useful information should generally use an empty alt attribute.

File names should also be descriptive. Names such as home-office-sunrise.webp are easier to understand and maintain than generic names such as image-final-v3.png.

Metadata requires additional consideration. Image-processing tools may remove metadata by default to reduce file size. This can include information that a project needs to preserve, depending on its requirements.

Before removing metadata, developers should review whether the website or client requires attribution, provenance information, or other embedded details.

After implementing an optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Chrome DevTools provides useful information about image requests.

Open Developer Tools and select the Network panel.

Resize the viewport or use device emulation.

Check whether the browser downloads appropriately sized images.

Developers can also inspect the image selected by the browser through the console:

This returns the current image URL selected for that element.

For websites with multiple images, inspect the relevant elements individually.

Finally, run an audit using Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. These tools can identify issues involving oversized images, image formats, loading priorities, and other performance factors.

Image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, JavaScript, and third-party scripts can also influence loading speed.

Several mistakes can reduce the effectiveness of an image optimization workflow:

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one format always produces the smallest file.

Omitting the sizes attribute from responsive images.

Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

Applying excessive compression and damaging visual details.

Removing metadata without checking project requirements.

Measuring file size without inspecting the final visual quality.

A consistent testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

No. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but the results depend on the image, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best way to choose an appropriate option.

Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of the page should generally load promptly.

The fundamental techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, AI-generated visuals may contain complex textures, gradients, and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design and make it easier to create custom visual content. However, efficient delivery requires more than exporting an image and uploading it to a website.

Developers should choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive image delivery. Including image dimensions helps prevent layout shifts, while appropriate loading priorities can improve the experience for visitors.

By testing images across different devices and reviewing their actual performance, development teams can maintain visual quality while reducing unnecessary downloads.

A repeatable optimization workflow makes it easier to publish new visuals without sacrificing website speed, accessibility, or reliability.

#10630. How Mastercard’s Michael Miebach learned to love collaboration

Hello and welcome to Modern CEO! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of Inc. and Fast Company. If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can sign up to get it yourself every Monday morning.

I may have been wearing a surgical mask the first time I shook hands with Michael Miebach. In June 2021, Mastercard invited me to its headquarters to interview Miebach, who’d become chief executive officer in January. At that point, much of the business world, including Mastercard, had started returning to their offices post-pandemic, but indoor masking and social distancing were still commonplace. (In this video we look like we’re about six feet apart from each other.) 

Miebach navigated Mastercard through the end of the pandemic. Since then, he has diversified beyond consumer credit cards into businesses such as data, insights, digital identities, and stablecoins, growing revenue from $18.9 billion in 2021 to $32.8 billion in 2025—and analysts expect 2026 revenue to top $37 billion. 

I recently caught up with Miebach (no mask this time) and asked him what he’s better at today than five years ago when we first met. He says he’s embraced the power of collaboration. Before becoming president of Mastercard, he was chief product officer, where he was “just doing stuff for us.” As CEO, he has come to appreciate the importance of the payments ecosystem working. “It comes down to changing [my] mindset from ‘I want to compete and differentiate only’ to ‘I want to compete and collaborate.’” 

AI opportunities—and limitations 

Miebach says cross-industry cooperation is alive and well in Mastercard’s efforts to support agentic commerce, in which artificial intelligence agents find the optimal product on behalf of humans. The agents proved great at research, and even negotiating deals, but completing transactions has been more elusive. Miebach says Mastercard’s approach has been to treat agents as an additional partner in the payments ecosystem, which traditionally has consisted of the cardholder, the bank that issues the card, the merchant, and the acquiring bank, which allows the merchant to accept payments. Card networks such as Mastercard and Visa link the parties together. 

In early 2025, the company launched Mastercard Agent Pay in the U.S. to integrate AI agents into the checkout process. In June, the company launched Agent Pay for Machines (AP4M), which aims to let agents transact with other agents continuously and at very high speeds. In announcing AP4M, Mastercard highlighted 31 participants, many of them fintech companies, underscoring the role of partnership. 

To be sure, there are also other coalitions and cooperatives being formed in the agentic commerce space, and different standards are emerging, too. There are competing payments protocols for payment authorization, for example. 

Leading through change 

Miebach believes the broader payments ecosystem will eventually coalesce around a set of standards, much the way companies came together around the Apple Pay digital wallet. 

And while it took Apple Pay, introduced in 2014, more than half a decade to become nearly ubiquitous, today 80% of Mastercard’s in-person transactions globally are contactless. Miebach is optimistic that agentic purchases, a “tiny” amount of the 180 billion transactions Mastercard processes annually, are poised to accelerate once industry players are aligned on regulations, tech standards, loyalty points integrations, and, crucially, systems that engender trust among consumers. Such systems include “know your agent” software that verifies that an AI agent is acting on behalf of a customer, as well as fraud monitoring and the ability to challenge unauthorized purchases. 

Indeed, for Miebach, agentic commerce isn’t just theoretical. He mentions during our meeting that he used an agent to make a purchase that day. The purchase—printer paper—wasn’t exciting or expensive, but, importantly, he says, “It worked.” 

Another thing that has changed for Miebach since taking the top job at Mastercard more than five years ago: He says he’s more comfortable with change and uncertainty. COVID was a lesson in leading without a playbook, and the fast pace of change means executives don’t always have all the answers. In fact, employees and leaders alike are often learning as they go, especially when working in fast-moving technologies such as agentic commerce. It’s another mindset shift Miebach has adopted. Today, he says, “I can [operate] much better with not having an answer.”

#10628. ‘I am deeply sorry’: Nvidia stock falls as Jensen Huang’s affair and an alleged spying scandal rocks the AI industry

Shares in Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) are sinking today, less than 12 hours after CEO Jensen Huang publicly confirmed that he’d had an extramarital affair, and after the chipmaker confirmed that it was investigating Huang’s relationship amid reports that the woman he’d had an affair with was allegedly spying on behalf of Beijing.

The story has rocked the AI industry at a time when related tech stocks are already facing their most significant headwinds since the artificial intelligence boom first took off. Here’s everything you need to know to get caught up.

Huang and Nvidia confirm affair and investigation

Last night, Nvidia published a statement from its board of directors confirming that the company has launched an independent investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang.

The statement came following earlier reports by the New York Times and the Financial Times alleging that Huang had been having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a senior leader at a Singapore-based cloud company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence services believe the woman was spying on behalf of China, the reports said.

Nvidia makes the world’s most advanced chips and graphics cards, which are now the backbone of the AI revolution.

For years, the company’s most state-of-the-art technology has faced export restrictions to China over national security fears. The United States and China are locked in an AI arms race, and U.S. lawmakers and national security experts worry that the sale of Nvidia’s hardware to China would give the country an edge economically and militarily.

While the extramarital affair stands to damage Huang’s personal reputation, AI industry insiders, Wall Street, and security experts are most concerned about the fact that Huang’s companion may have also been working as an intelligence operative.

There are fears that any industry information or Nvidia secrets that Jensen Huang may have discussed with Alice Huang could have been passed along to foreign intelligence services.

After Huang confirmed the affair—and Nvidia confirmed the investigation—Nvidia’s stock sank in premarket trading on Monday. This is more bad news for investors who have already seen AI-related stocks get hammered in the past week.

Fast Company reached out to Megaspeed for comment. It was not immediately clear if Alice Huang, who could not be reached for comment, still worked there.

What has Jensen Huang said?

When reports of the affair first broke, Jensen Huang suggested that he’d had only had normal business engagements with Alice Huang. The two had been photographed together at multiple business and social events.

But last night, Huang sent an email to Nvidia employees confirming the affair. Nvidia later published the message on its website. 

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” the message began. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Addressing Nvidia employees directly, Huang said, “you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Huang also addressed the national security concerns about his affair, saying the company had launched an independent investigation.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang added.

Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, has been seen as one of the single most influential tech leaders behind the AI revolution.

What has Nvidia said?

Nvidia confirmed that its board of directors has initiated an independent investigation into the reports that Huang may have “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” 

The investigation will be led by “independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel,” according to the company, with the board noting that it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

The company also stated that its board of directors has no reason to believe the company’s secrets or national security were compromised. 

Nvidia says that it still has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

What have China and the U.S. said?

Officials in China were quick to dispute the reports that it targeted Nvidia’s CEO in any way. Reuters quoted Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun as saying, “The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.”

As for U.S. officials, when reporters asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the matter, he replied: “Yeah, I can’t comment on any of that. I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.  And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.”

President Trump told reporters, “I have not spoken to [Jensen Huang] about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.” He added: ”I hope everything’s fine.”

The president also said, “I think he’s an honorable guy,” noting that the Nvidia CEO had “done an amazing job for our country.”

How has NVDA stock reacted?

Not well. As of this writing, in premarket trading, Nvidia shares are down more than 5% to just above $177. If today’s premarket drop holds, Nvidia will have lost more than 26% of its value in the past month alone.

Like many AI-related stocks last week, Nvidia shares sank in the days after the 2026 U.S. midterm election results, amid fears that the incoming Democratic-led Congress would take a more cautious approach to AI data center buildouts than the current administration. Voters have overwhelmingly shown their distaste for the massive server farms.

Huang’s scandal is sure to do no favors to the larger AI industry, which is already facing worries about a stock market bubble and growing unpopularity with the broader public.

What happens next?

Nvidia likely won’t be the only entity investigating the allegations.

Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, told CNBC, “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”

Ives believes there is a risk Jensen could be removed from his CEO position at Nvidia. 

“[T]his will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”

#10626. How veterans can help employers design better workplaces

November is the “official” month when America thanks our veterans for their bravery and service. However, it should also be the month when employers candidly ask themselves if they know what it takes to recruit, hire, and retain them. It’s true that veterans are broadly employed, with an unemployment rate of 3.5% in 2025 compared with 4.2% for nonveterans. What’s less evident, however, is whether current workforce systems fully recognize and tap veterans’ skills to help them secure quality jobs so they can better care for themselves and their families.

At the Ares Charitable Foundation, we fund efforts to prepare and reskill individuals for careers as a means to financial well-being, particularly for groups—including former military—that face unique employment barriers. Although the research points out their relatively low unemployment rate, we still need to examine the labor market challenges veterans experience as they transition from military to civilian life. Examining where and how conventional approaches fall short can reveal what redesigns are necessary if we want to build people-first systems.

TRANSLATE VETERAN SKILLS FOR IN-DEMAND JOBS

For many veterans, the first hurdle to mount is not lack of skills. Instead, it’s the difficult feat of translating military experience into a checklist that maps neatly onto job descriptions and résumés. The task of translating military service into terms that hiring managers and AI screening tools recognize usually falls to veterans themselves. They have to explain not just what they did, but also how it can add value for an employer. Research on veteran employment has identified this skills-matching challenge even within companies actively recruiting former military.

Despite this disconnect, veterans undeniably bring many of the capabilities businesses increasingly value. This is especially true as the workforce undergoes a major shift in the skills employers need. Leadership, decision-making, communication, teamwork, problem-solving, and the ability to perform under pressure while adapting to changing circumstances are all competencies that translate across industries and roles. These make veterans a significant workforce asset. However, failure to prioritize these kinds of highly transferable skills can create missed opportunities to smartly leverage veterans’ unique assets.

BETTER HIRING IS ONLY THE BEGINNING

Recruitment is only one piece of the puzzle. Companies wanting to build more viable pathways to support service members’ transitions from military to civilian employment should probe what shapes the employee experience from hiring through career development. It is especially critical at this watershed moment. A new RAND study finds that available data often can’t show whether efforts of America’s largest companies translate into enduring, positive career outcomes for veterans. This despite the public commitments to support them.

This dearth of data makes clear that employers need to design, test, and scale strategies that recognize and develop veterans’ talents even after they land  jobs. This includes ensuring effective onboarding and talent development for continued learning and career development. The U.S. Department of Labor suggests tailored career development initiatives like skills building in leadership, civilian communication styles, and adapting military skills to the private sector. For employers, this necessitates equipping recruiters and hiring managers to better correlate skills with military experience. It also requires devising people-centered processes that facilitate employees’ abilities to identify and access tailored resources that help them achieve workplace success.

DESIGN FOR DISABILITIES TO BUILD BETTER SYSTEMS

The imperative for workforce systems redesign is even more important for veterans with disabilities. Around 34% of U.S. veterans contends with a service-related disability, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, representing a significant and frequently overlooked segment of labor market participants. While that may seem like a staggering metric, those who live the reality don’t always fit neatly into conventional veteran employment programs or standard disability-inclusion strategies. This leaves them underserved by both.

Closing this gap requires a more coordinated approach to talent development. Furthermore, that the gap even exists reveals an opportunity and responsibility employers have to strengthen their veteran employment and disability inclusion strategies. They should identify and mitigate impediments that hinder current employees and those they may otherwise miss out on hiring.

Ares Charitable Foundation is partnering s with Disability:IN to publish a report that offers a disability-forward analysis of veterans’ employment. The new research is part of an initiative that will also engage chief human resources officers in problem-solving challenges to recruiting, hiring, supporting, and retaining disabled veterans. In the future, these efforts will include a practical, actionable, and evidence-based playbook to better ensure disabled veterans’ workplace success.

HONOR SERVICE IN WAYS THAT MATTER MOST

With roughly 200,000 service members looking to transition into civilian roles each year, the time to rethink how employers welcome and support them is now. The lesson is bigger than simply hiring more veterans. Rather, it includes what employers need to understand about designing workforce systems around people rather than processes. That allows them to recognize the many different forms in which experience, skills, and capability come.

November, National Veterans and Military Families Month, marks an opportunity for our country to do more than just thank those who have served. We can help make the military-to-civilian workforce transition more seamless, and also truly honor their service by championing tangible opportunities for them to achieve economic mobility. 

Michelle Armstong is president of the Ares Charitable Foundation.

#10625. Samsung’s Android XR ‘Intelligent Eyewear’ reportedly launches in December

Samsung smart glasses in Gentle Monster and Warby Parker styles may finally launch in South Korea and the US before Christmas.

It’s been a very long time coming, but one report from ChoSun Biz says that Samsung and Google are finally launching the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear line in the United States and South Korea in mid-December. Curiously, while the report helps set a fuzzy date, there’s still no official price for Samsung’s smart glasses.

Back in July, Samsung teased the price, noting that the company’s first smart glasses will come in at “a reasonable price” for a product “in the premium range.” Presumably, that means Samsung Intelligent Eyewear won’t be shipping at $299 like Meta’s latest smart glasses. Meta’s most premium offering, Oakley Meta Vanguard, retails for $499.

All of the upcoming Samsung Intelligent Eyewear models feature cameras on the front, although it’s possible Samsung will release camera-free glasses sometime in the future.

Even at a similar price, Samsung hopes its glasses will differentiate themselves from Meta’s offerings by being “an extension of the experience centered on the smartphone, rather than being a post-smartphone device.” Meta has been developing wearable computers for a while now, including VR and lighter XR headsets, often citing that they’re devices for the post-smartphone era. Samsung, instead, sees its glasses as a companion to phones, similar to smartwatches.

Samsung Intelligent Eyewear also has the advantage of having Gemini onboard and running Android XR, the official Google-built operating system for smart glasses and VR headsets. That means it’s sure to tie in with your Android-powered smartphone better than anything else on the market, something we’ve seen from Wear OS smartwatches.
