#10624. Turn individual experimentation into organizational learning

AI adoption is accelerating, but adoption doesn’t equal workplace transformation.

According to Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace 2026 report, 65% of workers in U.S. organizations that have implemented AI say the technology has had some degree of positive impact on their individual productivity. That’s an encouraging sign, until you consider that only 12% strongly agree that AI has transformed how work gets done.

That gap points to the next challenge for leaders. Many of AI’s early gains have centered on helping individuals complete existing work faster. The bigger opportunity is figuring out how what one employee learns can change how an entire team, function, or organization works.

Today, two employees sitting directly across from each other can have dramatically different experiences with the same AI tool. While one might use the technology to write an email, the other may have discovered a way to redesign a process that saves significant time and resources. If those use cases stay with the individuals, the organization never captures their full value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded across organizations, access to the technology itself is less likely to create sustainable advantage. The real differentiator will be how quickly organizations can turn what employees learn into shared knowledge, redesigned workflows, and better ways of working.

LEADERS SET THE DIRECTION

Because employees are closest to day-to-day work, they’re often uncovering the most practical ways AI can improve work or solve problems differently. They understand where existing processes create friction and where AI might enable a better approach.

Walmart provides one useful example. Rather than treating employees only as end users of AI, the company has involved them in shaping AI applications. One logistics manager helped create an AI process designed to improve truck efficiency and reduce empty trailers. The insight did not originate with someone studying the workflow from a distance. It came from someone close enough to the work to see what needed to change.

Leaders can create the conditions for that type of discovery by establishing the problems worth solving, setting the boundaries for experimentation, and defining what a better outcome looks like. Employees then have room to figure out how AI can change work.

At my company, Cengage, we introduced AI in phases. Our “Change Champions” across the company experimented with AI, identified meaningful use cases, and shared what they learned with their teams. This shared-learning model allowed us to build knowledge across the organization. As access expanded, employees had examples, practices, and colleagues they could learn from rather than asking every team to start from scratch. Now, nearly 90% of employees with access are actively using AI.

Experimentation creates far more value when the knowledge it produces can travel beyond the individual or team that discovered it.

MAKE LEARNING PART OF THE OPERATING MODEL

One employee finding a better way to perform a task creates individual productivity. Dozens of employees learning from that discovery, adapting it to their own work, and improving it creates organizational impact.

Organizations need a way for those discoveries to travel across departments. Employees should be able to share what they’ve tried and what they’ve learned, giving other teams a starting point for their own experimentation.

At Canva last year, 5,000 employees were given a dedicated week to learn and experiment with AI, and to explore how the technology could improve their work. The value of creating the space extends beyond what employees accomplished during that week. It created an opportunity for what they learned, to spread across the entire organization.

Traditional training still helps employees build a shared foundation and understand how to use AI responsibly. But training alone can’t keep pace with a technology that is changing this quickly. The most useful applications often emerge as employees try AI against the real challenges in their work. Organizations need to make it easy for those employees to share what they’ve learned, so a promising idea can become a starting point for others. At Cengage, we saw the value of that approach through our Change Champions. Employees with subject matter expertise learned by experimenting, then brought practical examples back to their teams.

MANAGERS BRIDGE EXPERIMENTATION AND SCALE

In addition to encouraging employees to experiment, a culture of shared learning requires giving employees the time and support to test new ideas and share what they learn without expecting every experiment to demonstrate an immediate return.

Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index found that when managers created psychological safety around experimentation, employees reported up to 20 points higher AI readiness and value.

Senior leaders can set the expectation that AI experimentation is important, but employees experience culture primarily through their managers. That puts managers in an increasingly important position. They can protect time for experimentation, help teams identify worthwhile problems, set expectations for quality and responsible use, and make sharing lessons part of the team’s regular work. They are also close enough to distinguish between an interesting demo and a change that genuinely improves a workflow. They are the bridge between individual experimentation and organizational learning.

BUILD A COMPANY THAT CONTINUOUSLY LEARNS

The next phase of AI adoption is an organizational learning challenge. Models will change. Tools will change. What seemed like a leading-edge use case six months ago may quickly become commonplace.

Organizations cannot retrain the entire workforce from scratch every time that happens. They need a system that helps employees iterate to discover, test, share, and build on better ways of working.

The organizations that ultimately create the most value from AI will build the capacity to continually learn what the technology makes possible—and turn those individual discoveries into better ways of working across the organization.

Darren Person is EVP and chief product and digital officer at Cengage.

#10622. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.

#10621. How trust and governance make or break AI investments

I’ve had the privilege of working with some brilliant colleagues throughout my career. But the strongest professional relationships, especially in the C-suite, aren’t built overnight. They’re built over time on a foundation of trust and a clear understanding of roles, responsibilities, and decision-making authority.

The same principle applies to AI. People won’t rely on AI systems unless they understand and trust the information and decisions behind them. And for AI to deliver meaningful results, it needs a strong foundation.

That foundation has two essential components. The first is a single, trusted source of truth. That means one authoritative record that determines which system prevails when data conflicts arise, identifies who owns each asset, and shows whether it is compliant at any given moment. The second is governance: clear decisions made in advance about where human oversight is required before an automated action can proceed.

In short, the foundation requires data you can trust and a live human in the loop.

You might have gotten away with delaying those decisions in the past. Not anymore, because the money is already spent. Our recent survey shows that 56% of organizations are implementing AI broadly across different workflows or at the scale where the business depends on it. Just 2% of those surveyed reported not using AI at all. Similar to relationships in your career, automation must be built on clear understanding, which builds trust.

AI CAN RECOMMEND, BUT NOT ANSWER FOR THE RESULT

AI does a good job processing information and recommending actions when it can pull information from a trusted system of record. It cannot establish or verify what exists in your environment, who owns it, what it connects to, what changed last month, or whether any of it would survive an audit. Those are matters of record, and someone has to keep the record and be accountable for it.

Fortunately, creating that record is a more practical process than many organizations realize. Start with discovery—an authoritative inventory of what exists across every environment. Attach ownership and lifecycle to each asset to identify them. Keep the change history, because that is what an auditor asks for. Then decide which system wins when the two systems disagree, and document that answer.

That process tends to crystallize too late for many teams, like when an auditor asks how a change was approved. Nobody wants the answer to be that the system recommended it.

FIRST, SORT ACTIONS INTO TWO PILES

Some teams are already scrambling to cover for this. In our survey, which included 1,500 IT professionals, 68% said they had seen AI create a hallucination with potential operational impact. Just over half said a team member caught it before it caused problems; 16% said that hallucinations caused issues.

For a lot of companies, that catch rate is the entire control framework. Catching stuff is great, but this framework depends on the right person being alert at the right moment. That’s not how to run a business.

Instead, sort actions into two piles before anything goes live. The first pile is routine and reversible work that can run on its own. This includes restarting a service or applying a standard patch. The second pile is anything that changes a system-wide setting or touches a live incident. That should undergo human review. After sorting them, write each group into the workflow rather than leaving it to individual judgment.

Don’t mistake this being handled on paper for being handled in real life. Our survey found 85% of IT professionals saying that every AI agent and workflow has a named owner in their organization. But only 42% say that ownership is clear in practice. Where policies exist, just 24% of employees say they are followed very consistently.

GUARDRAILS HELP ACCELERATE GOOD DECISIONS

You might have read the last few paragraphs and thought, “This sounds like more tedious governance.” To be fair, governance was the most common answer IT professionals gave in our survey when asked what slows their AI deployment; 27% name governance, security, or compliance, ahead of skills shortages and technology limits.

But I believe the problem is how governance is run, not governance itself. Think of AI governance as setting expectations and managing accountability in a working relationship. It removes uncertainty and provides clarity.

Settled rules about data, ownership, and human review take the debate out of most requests, speeding up approvals. I would rather spend a few weeks setting those boundaries than spend the year approving things one at a time.

WHAT YOU GET FOR YOUR TROUBLE

I understand if this feels both oversimplified (Trustworthy data! Keep a human in the loop!) and cumbersome (Fix your framework! Sort! Audit! Document!). But it really comes down to a bit of up-front effort for a significant payoff that can arrive faster than you might think.

IT professionals using AI at the most advanced level said in our survey that they save an average of six hours a week—double what their peers at the earliest stage save—and half say AI is freeing them up for more complex, strategic work.

Trusted data and a human in the loop let you widen an AI program with confidence instead of widening it and hoping. It’s also what allows you to confidently invest in more comprehensive, end-to-end automation systems that can improve flow without extra headaches, because you’re building on solid ground.

So, if you are deciding where to put resources in the next quarter, I would skip a bolted-on tool. Test all this with one workflow you already depend on. Reconcile what your systems say about the assets it touches. Then decide who signs off on what. Do that a few times and you’ll have both things in place: a record you trust and people positioned where it counts. While others keep bolting on and reacting, you’ll be setting up for fewer headaches, streamlined operations, and more confident decisions.

Melissa Puls is chief marketing officer and SVP of customer success and renewals at Ivanti.

#10618. Public services embrace Big Tech

Palantir has drawn scrutiny for supplying systems that public agencies use to integrate and analyze data about people’s lives, from health to security and economic administration.

In June, Reuters reported that Britain was reviewing its £330 million NHS contract over concerns about confidentiality, public trust, and dependence on a U.S. supplier, alongside reported improvements in waiting lists and hospital discharges. In May 2025, The New York Times reported that Palantir engineers were organizing IRS taxpayer data using Foundry. Last year, the Washington Post also documented Palantir’s expanding military and immigration enforcement work.

Yet Palantir’s everyday reach remains narrower than Microsoft’s, Google’s, or Meta’s. For decades, Microsoft and Google have served people worldwide, across languages, with tools for education, communication, and office work. They have become part of the infrastructure of daily life.

Less clear is these companies’ intent to become integral to citizens’ institutional lives through government itself. For the past 120 days, I have followed Google’s footprint across several of Brazil’s 26 states. São Paulo, for instance, is roughly the size of Oregon. Its preliminary 2025 GDP, converted at the annual average exchange rate, would place it 15th among U.S. state economies, behind Virginia and Michigan.

I selected three states for comparison: São Paulo, Paraná, and Mato Grosso. Together, they had 61.6 million residents and generated approximately $90.5 billion in agricultural production value in 2024. This exceeded the reported output of Germany ($81.7 billion), Italy ($81.6 billion), and the Netherlands ($44.6 billion), approaching France’s $96.7 billion. Google provides infrastructure and information services for these state governments.

GOOGLE’S EXPANDING ROLE IN PARANÁ

At Paraná’s state government headquarters recently, José Padilha walked me through Google’s growing role in education, healthcare, agriculture, and public administration. As director of artificial intelligence at the state’s Secretariat of Innovation and Artificial Intelligence, he shared how he had brought the company into these areas.

Celepar, the state’s government technology company, serves as a distribution partner for Google’s infrastructure and services across departments and agencies. Although the contract may not make the broader intent explicit, the arrangement embeds Google throughout state operations.

Paraná’s AI-First strategy spans 52 departments and agencies, consolidating government data into a central repository of structured and semi-structured information. At the time of our conversation, he said the government provided 5,000 licenses for Google’s LLM chat application to its employees and deployed 1,316 autonomous applications powered by large language models, known as AI agents. Padilha plans to expand access to 36,000 employees—30% of the state workforce—and extend services to all 399 municipalities.

The strategy includes projects applying Google’s technology to specific public services, from emergency management and agriculture to healthcare, policing, and migrant integration.

A CLOSER LOOK AT PARANÁ’S PUBLIC SERVICE PROJECTS

These state projects use Google’s technology to support specific public services.

PRISMA, an emergency management platform, combines weather imagery, historical and geospatial data, contingency plans, and municipal records on land use, population, and property. It aims to connect past events with current weather conditions and identify resources for timely responses.

Paraná Mais Sustentável, a platform for agricultural and environmental services, involves Google directly in its core technology and data processing. It integrates land use planning and rural services, combining records from approximately 300,000 agricultural operations with state agency data. Functions include rural addressing, route mapping, agricultural and environmental certificates, and analysis of data on native vegetation loss from PRODES, Brazil’s official satellite deforestation monitoring system, operated by the National Institute for Space Research. It also supports environmental reserve policies and certifications that may affect access to international markets.

Project Capricorn, an AI initiative brought by Google through a European partnership, uses a PubMed-derived dataset prepared for machine learning to support cancer case analysis in public hospitals.

The Intelligent Virtual Police Station, a state police service using Google’s technology, helps residents file police reports through a conversational interface, structuring facts for police review. Its current role focuses on operational support. G-Migra, a state migration management platform also using Google’s technology, organizes data for the Justice and Citizenship Department to plan and monitor migrant reception and integration policies.

Padilha is enthusiastic about the results, reporting substantial benefits for residents. My own observations also point to improvements and strong public approval. According to Padilha, Google executives and affiliated suppliers work directly with government teams, and five other Brazilian states are considering adoption. Google maintains a sales team in Brazil to support this expansion.

BIG TECH: STRENGTHEN OR DISPLACE THE STATE?

At Google’s invitation, I attended an event in São Paulo last September, where Padilha presented Paraná’s projects to attendees. There, I saw how Google organizes its commercial efforts to serve governments as customers, with dedicated sales executives and formal industry divisions covering education, the public sector, telecommunications, healthcare, and energy and natural resources.

Google may already be embedded in public infrastructure across dozens of countries beyond the familiar markets of the developed world, attracting less attention along the way. A preliminary search identified contracts, procurement initiatives, and partnerships in Chile, Malaysia, Kuwait, Israel, and Rwanda, as well as an agreement with the African Union Commission. These relationships suggest an increasingly pervasive institutional presence.

Data privacy remains an essential concern. Alongside that discussion, however, lies an institutional question: As technology companies become integral to public services, how might they change the state’s capacity, authority, and legitimacy?

We may be observing the formation of a horizontal position that spans national borders, bringing together new combinations of data and populations. In this sense, “informational countries” could emerge across the fixed geographic boundaries of existing states. But concluding that this development has harmed, or will harm, those populations would require evidence we do not yet have. The full impact on residents remains difficult to measure.

Information now moves faster than the administrative snapshots through which the modern state, shaped in the twentieth century, understands its population and economy. Businesses operate at that speed, potentially changing how we classify economic activities in the years ahead.

From a system dynamics perspective, faster and richer information can improve the feedback through which institutions adjust their decisions. Whether this produces better outcomes depends on how that information is interpreted and acted upon. There is reason for optimism, but the result is not automatic.

Google’s expanding infrastructure also creates opportunities for developers around the world. Their ability to turn those opportunities into services that improve people’s lives will be an important measure of what these relationships ultimately deliver.

Rodrigo Magnago is director at RMagnago Critical Thinking.

#10616. How to Test AI-Generated Content Before It Reaches Your Users

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams now ship something an AI helped write: help-center articles, product descriptions, release notes, even code comments. The draft appears in seconds, and that speed is the trap. Nobody tests it the way they would test a new feature, so mistakes slip through that a quick review would have caught.

This guide is about the other side of AI testing. Instead of using AI to test your software, you test what AI hands you. Here is a simple routine that fits into a normal publishing or release process.

AI writing sounds confident whether or not it is right. A model can invent a statistic (researchers call this hallucination and have documented it across many text-generation systems), quote a feature your product does not have, or describe a setting that was renamed two releases ago. The sentence reads smoothly, so the error hides in plain sight.

Traditional QA does not cover this. A unit test tells you the page loads. It says nothing about whether the claim on the page is true. That gap is where most AI-related incidents begin.

1. Define what "good" means before you generate anything. Write down the audience, the claims you are willing to make and the sources you trust. A short brief makes the output easier to judge, because you are comparing it with something concrete.

2. Check every factual claim. Highlight each number, name and statement of fact, then verify it against a primary source. Google's own guidance on generative AI content tells publishers to fact-check AI output, including titles, descriptions and alt text, before publishing. If you cannot confirm a claim in a minute or two, cut it or rewrite it as something you can support.

3. Test the instructions. For tutorials and how-to content, follow the steps exactly as written on a clean machine or account. Commands that fail and menus that no longer exist show up immediately this way.

4. Review the voice. Replace vague phrases with specifics from your own experience: a real customer question, a real error message, a real number from your analytics. This is also what separates useful content from filler.

5. Keep a human owner. Every piece should have a named person who approved it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework makes the same point at organization level: people stay accountable for how AI is used and evaluated. If something goes wrong later, you know who to ask and where to fix it.

Some teams also run drafts through an AI detector. That can be useful as a prompt for a closer look, for example when freelancers or vendors deliver work and you want to know how much of it was machine-generated. A high score is a reason to read more carefully. It is not proof of anything, and it should never decide an outcome on its own, because detectors make mistakes in both directions. A Stanford study found that GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, and short texts are easy to misjudge too. If you want a quick second opinion on a draft, a tool like Tester AI can give you a starting point for that conversation.

Review works best when it is not optional. A few small habits make it stick.

Treating the first draft as finished. It is a starting point. Plan time for review the same way you plan time for writing.

Reviewing for grammar only. Clean sentences are not evidence of correct content. Check meaning first and polish second.

Letting the tool grade its own work. Asking the same model to confirm its answer rarely catches real errors. Use a source or a person.

Skipping legal and brand review. Generated text can echo existing material or make promises your company cannot keep. Anything customer-facing deserves a second pair of eyes.

AI can save hours of drafting, but speed only helps if the result is trustworthy. Treat generated content like code from a new contributor: useful, often good, and always reviewed before it goes live. A short routine of defining quality, verifying facts, testing instructions and keeping a human owner will catch most problems before your users do.

Do I need to test AI-generated content if a human edits it? Yes. Editing for style does not confirm that the facts are correct. Verify claims separately from polishing the wording.

How long should a review take? For a typical article, expect roughly the time it takes to read it twice plus a few minutes per factual claim. Reviews are faster when the brief and sources are prepared in advance.

Can an AI detector prove that text was written by a machine? No. Detectors estimate likelihood, and they can be wrong. Use the result as a signal for human review, never as the final decision.

What should I check first? Start with numbers, names, dates and anything a customer could act on, such as prices, steps or legal statements. Those carry the highest risk if they are wrong.

#10615. Healthy futures start early

If you ask anyone what they want for their children, you’ll likely hear one of the same answers continue to pop up: good health.

However, childhood health outcomes are heading in the wrong direction. About one in five children and adolescents in the U.S. has obesity, and recent research published in JAMA found that several measures of children’s health have declined since 2007, including sleep health, mental health, and chronic physical conditions.

These trends have consequences that extend well beyond childhood. Research shows that many of the chronic diseases driving healthcare costs, straining employers, and reducing workforce productivity are influenced by habits and routines established during early childhood. These conditions include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension. They also affect working families today, as parents navigate the challenges of supporting a child’s health while balancing work responsibilities.

If we want healthier adults and a more productive workforce tomorrow, we need to invest in healthier habits for children today.

A POWERFUL PREVENTION OPPORTUNITY

Organizations across healthcare, education, government, and the nonprofit sector have long recognized the importance of helping children live healthier lives. There are many longstanding health programs for elementary and high school-age children, such as Action for Healthy Kids and Abbott’s own Future Well Kids, along with federally supported programs such as Bright Futures. All are working toward the same goal.

While school-age health is important, experts increasingly identify early childhood, as young as three years old, as a critical window for development. This is when habits begin to take shape and can influence health outcomes for years to come. By the time children start kindergarten, many of the routines that shape their daily lives are already established.

That thinking led to Abbott’s collaboration with Sesame Workshop. By combining health expertise with a trusted voice in early childhood education, the shared effort aims to reach more families with practical tools and resources that can help make healthy habits easier to build and maintain from an early age.

For young children, healthy routines around nutrition, movement, and sleep may feel more approachable and fun when coming from a beloved character like Elmo rather than another reminder from an adult—including lessons about trying a new food or developing a bedtime routine.

To reach families with young children, it’s important to meet them where they are with tools they can seamlessly integrate into their everyday lives.

MAKE HEALTHY HABITS WORK FOR REAL LIFE

Most families are already aware that healthy habits matter. They understand that nutrition, movement, and sleep play an important role in lifelong well-being. The harder task is turning that knowledge into action for working parents amid work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, financial pressures, and the competing demands of family life.

A recent survey we conducted with Kantar earlier this year reflects this challenge. Nearly all of the 2,000 parents surveyed said childhood habits influence lifelong health, yet many also reported feeling significant pressure to model healthy behaviors while experiencing difficulty doing so consistently.

This gap between knowing and doing is one of the most persistent challenges in public health.

Information is essential, but it is rarely enough on its own. Lasting behavior change happens when healthy choices are convenient, accessible, and realistic for families.

INVEST IN THE NEXT GENERATION

That’s why successful interventions focus less on perfection and more on building small, sustainable habits that fit into everyday routines. The opportunity now is to bring businesses, nonprofits, educators, and families together to make health a natural part of the programs and spaces that already support young children.

Supporting children’s health is an investment in stronger communities, a healthier future workforce, and better long-term outcomes. Organizations that help remove barriers for families can contribute to healthier generations for years to come.

Every small step taken together can help set the foundation for lifelong health and reverse the rise of chronic disease.

Melissa Brotz is senior vice president of global marketing and external affairs for Abbott, and president of Abbott Fund.

Is it faster to repurpose multiple small sites than to build one massive data center?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Internet and telecommunications provider Brightspeed is reportedly in talks with Nvidia to convert several of its buildings into tiny data centers. According to The Information, Nvidia pitched the idea to Apollo Global Management executives, the parent company of Brightspeed, who then asked it to submit written plans to the internet provider. Nvidia complied and has now requested additional information, data, and site visits to some of Brightspeed’s existing infrastructure.

The telecommunications company has around 130 buildings located around the country, many of which are already built to handle data and voice traffic and have the required power infrastructure to run Nvidia servers. Sources say that the AI tech giant estimates that these sites could collectively deliver around 1 gigawatt of compute capacity, which could accommodate more than 2,200 Supermicro Vera Rubin NVL72 racks containing 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs each. Although these sites already can power these GPUs, it’s still not a plug-and-play solution, as Nvidia would still need to install cooling systems and other supporting architecture. These would still require permits and approval from the local government, but they would likely face less red tape and opposition compared to building a data center from the ground up.

Apollo Global Management has already made significant bets in AI hardware, with the asset management company involved in a $40 billion deal with SpaceX that would give it around 360,000 Vera Rubin GPUs across 5,000 NVL72 racks. While it’s currently unclear who will own the AI chips installed in Brightspeed facilities, the proposal could potentially help Apollo find a place for the Nvidia chips it ordered to get them up and running as soon as possible. This is a much better solution compared to waiting for years to get a data center approved, all while facing resistance from the community even after getting the go-ahead from the local government.

Having multiple small data centers like this is also a setup that OpenAI and Anthropic have been considering, especially as larger facilities are facing delays and backlash from the communities that they’re in. While having a large, homogeneous cluster built in one location is preferable for training, Nvidia representatives have described these smaller sites working together as an “inference network” to help run existing AI models. This is especially important as AI agents, which use five to ten times more tokens than humans, become more popular.

The move to use existing facilities instead of building new ones from scratch has received renewed attention, especially after Americans overwhelmingly voted against data centers during the midterm elections. While the more than 300 data center bans enacted across the U.S. have only delayed three existing projects, it’s feared that the bans and moratoriums would make it that much harder to start new data center developments and make it difficult for AI companies to secure the compute capacity needed to power their AI models in the future.

#10611. A major Venmo update could change how you pay for dinner with friends

Splitting the bill after a group dinner can sometimes feel like an Olympic sport. One friend ordered the expensive steak, their girlfriend stuck to a salad, and your friend Greg has been drinking expensive bourbon all night but thinks you should all just split the bill evenly.

Venmo is finally taking some of the mental gymnastics out of the equation.

The payment app is rolling out a new receipt-scanning feature this week that lets users take a photo of a receipt, automatically itemize everything on it, and assign individual charges to the people who ordered them.

How Venmo’s new receipt-scanning feature works

The new tool is built directly into the Venmo app, so users won’t need to download anything extra or switch between apps to split a bill.

To use it, open Venmo, tap the V on the home screen to start a payment, and select “Scan receipt.” From there, take a photo of the receipt or upload an existing image.

Venmo automatically identifies and itemizes the purchases. Users can then assign individual items to the appropriate people and make adjustments as needed. Once everything is assigned, Venmo calculates each person’s portion of the tax and tip and generates payment requests. The feature works regardless of which mobile device someone in the group uses.

“Splitting the bill is one of the most common things people do on Venmo, but it can also be one of the most tedious,” said Alexis Sowa, Venmo’s general manager. “With receipt scanning, a pile of math goes away with a single photo. Venmo does the heavy lifting so customers can get back to what matters: the meal, the trip, or the night out with friends.”

Gen Z is often stuck figuring out who owes what

The launch comes as new research from Venmo suggests younger adults often cover group expenses upfront and collect payments afterward.

In a survey conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of Venmo, 40% of adults aged 18 to 22 said they’re typically the person who pays first and then collects everyone else’s share.

The research also found that people have different approaches to dividing shared expenses.

About 20% of respondents said they split bills based on exactly what each person ordered, while 15% divide the total evenly. Another 12% said they take turns paying or have different people cover different portions of the bill. Meanwhile, 11% said one person typically pays the entire bill and requests everyone’s share afterward.

The findings suggest there’s no universally accepted way to split a group bill, which may be part of what makes the process so frustrating.

It’s not just for restaurant bills

Although splitting restaurant checks is an obvious use for the feature, Venmo says receipt scanning can also help people manage other shared expenses.

Roommates, for instance, could use it to divide a grocery receipt based on who purchased which items, rather than splitting the total evenly. Friends traveling together could scan receipts from meals or shared purchases to settle expenses after a trip.

The tool also works alongside Venmo Groups, an existing feature that allows users to track shared expenses over time.

Groups is designed for situations where people regularly split costs, whether roommates manage household purchases, couples divide monthly bills, or friends track expenses during a vacation. Instead of handling every expense as a separate transaction, users can see shared spending in one place and settle up when they’re ready.

When will Venmo’s receipt-scanning feature be available?

Venmo says the feature is rolling out now, with wider availability expected over the next several weeks. That means some users may see the option before others.

The launch is part of a broader Venmo app update designed to make its payment and financial features easier to find and use.

Other features highlighted in the updated app include scheduling recurring payments, such as monthly rent, and earning rewards through Venmo Stash.

For anyone who’s ever spent 15 minutes after dinner trying to figure out who owes $23.47, the new receipt scanner could be a welcome addition. The only thing it can’t do is persuade your friend to actually pay you back.

#10608. A celebrated Berlin designer turns her eye to kids’ furniture

If you walk through the kids’ furniture section of a Target or Walmart, you’ll get a glimpse into what adults think children like: pink for girls, blue for boys, a parade of cartoon bunnies and Disney princesses emblazoned on bed frames and step stools.

But do kids actually want all this? Or have we simply stereotyped them? Hanne Willmann suspects we underestimate children’s ability to appreciate clean, minimalist design. The Berlin-based industrial designer and founder of Studio Hanne Willmann has spent a decade making products for grown-ups: chairs and sofas for Freifrau, tables for Favius, lighting for Hartô Designs. Today, in an interesting twist, Willmann takes on the role of chief design officer for Piccalio, a six-year-old Los Angeles furniture startup.

Willmann’s new collection for Piccalio—a table and chair set made of carved wood—reflects her approach to designing for children. The pieces, which are inspired by a 1970s Swiss chair, blend the simplicity of wood with interesting curves. Willmann believes they will appeal to both parents and children, who will cultivate a taste for good design.

A European Approach

There’s a long history of European designers bringing their skills to children’s furniture. Alma Siedhoff-Buscher designed a suite of children’s furniture for a model house in a 1923 Bauhaus exhibition in Weimar, Germany, where every piece was multipurpose: a dresser cabinet became a puppet theater, a changing table became a writing desk.

In the 1930s, the Finnish designer Alvar Aalto designed a children’s version of his famous three-legged Artek stool, and it has been part of Scandinavian schools and nurseries for generations. And in Norway, Peter Opsvik’s Tripp Trapp chair for Stokke has become a global best-seller.

The founders of Piccalio—Ali Tavsanoglu and Aneta Kostic, a married couple who met in the U.K. and now live in L.A.—are inspired by this history of design. They launched the startup in 2020, after a frustrating afternoon shopping for furniture for their niece and nephews. A lot of products they found on the U.S. market were low quality, covered in graphics, and inconsistent with the aesthetics of a modern home.

For their first product, they wanted to create a safe step stool for children to help their parents in the kitchen. They developed a sturdy wooden “toddler tower” with a railing that lifts small children, so they can reach kitchen counters and sinks. They began modestly, selling the $249 product on Etsy, but it quickly became a breakout. So they decided to launch their own website, where they also sold a $499 bed that won awards from Domino and Good Housekeeping. The brand is sold as well at Babylist, Maisonette, and Janie and Jack. Since 2020, Piccalio has more than doubled its sales each year, and now generates upwards of $10 million in revenue.

Bringing on an Industrial Designer

The success of the toddler tower inspired Piccalio’s founders to have broader ambitions, and reimagine other children’s furniture.

In 2022, before bringing her on as their chief design officer, they partnered with Willmann to design other furniture. Willmann’s focus is on bringing out the natural beauty in the lines and materials of the material she’s using. She wants her objects to inspire feelings, like comfort, safety, or creativity. “My work sits somewhere between sensual and functional,” she says.

When it comes to children’s furniture, Willmann takes cues from Montessori education, where child-sized furniture inspires kids to move and work independently. She wants to create pieces that accomplish a task, but that are simple enough that children can find other uses for them. “If you give a child paper, they will draw something, or make a paper plane, or create a little basket to hold paper balls,” she says. “They are crazily creative if you don’t limit them.”

But Willmann finds many Montessori-based products to be clinical or overtly pedagogical. She believes it is possible to create furniture that supports kids’ learning and creativity that is also attractive and fun. This is evident in her first project for Piccalio, which was designing a toddler table and chair set that comes in a range of calm colors, like ochre yellow and sage green. While Piccalio doesn’t share revenue figures, Tavsanoglu says that sales of this table set exceeded expectations.

The furniture is easy for a child to manipulate, and the chair can be flipped upside down or on its side to create different ways of sitting. There is a little semicircle on the backrest that evokes a rainbow, but also serves as a handle to pick the chair up. With some imagination, toddlers can transform the table into a fort or turn it upside down to pretend it is a boat; the chair can become a little bed for a doll.

“They may not even sit on it,” says Willmann. “That’s the beautiful thing about kids. I would never want to limit what kids do with products like these.”

Curved Wood Table

In her role as chief design officer of Piccalio, Willmann has created a new table and chair set, called Arcc, designed for older children of preschool age. The idea is that children will graduate from the toddler set to this set as they spend more time doing crafts, drawing, and learning to write.

Its reference point is the wooden Rey chair, designed in 1971 by the Swiss designer Bruno Rey, which has a curved backrest, a circle seat, and rounded edges. (The Danish brand Hay now sells the chair, starting at $645.) Willmann’s version is similarly minimal, and aims to bring curved lines into the wooden furniture. There is an interesting visual contrast between the hardness of the wood and the gentle movement you sense from the arched back and legs.

The set is made from bentwood, thin layers of wood with alternating grain that are glued and pressed together with heat. This approach requires developing a complex and expensive mold. Piccalio partners with a Romanian factory that has specialized in this technique for 70 years. The proportions are scaled to a child’s body, rather than shrunk from an adult chair. And the rounded shapes are designed to look engaging, friendly and safe, without tipping into cartoonish. It comes in several wood finishes, as well as red and light blue.

At upwards of $650 for a table and two chairs, the Arcc set is pricey. But Tavsanoglu believes there is a growing market in the U.S. for aesthetically pleasing, durable children’s furniture that pushes back against the wave of “fast furniture” that is widely available on Amazon and Wayfair.

Piccalio is part of a small but growing group of design-oriented children’s brands, like New York-based Lalo, which makes toys and furniture, and Belgium’s EcoBirdy, which makes speckled chairs and tables from recycled plastic toys. Bauen sells an award-winning table-and-chair set engineered to resist tipping.

These brands charge more than mass market, and have proven that some parents are willing to pay for pieces that fit within their home’s aesthetic. Tavsanoglu says there’s now a booming secondhand market for high quality children’s furniture, and Piccalio expects its pieces to last years of play. “Often, our pieces show up on Facebook Marketplace for 80% of what they cost new,” he says.

Many of Piccalio’s customers live in big cities where they don’t have space to shove their children’s furniture into a playroom. Families want them to match the broader aesthetic of their living room or kitchen. For Willmann, small spaces are not a disadvantage; she believes they encourage families to spend more time together.

“It can be sad if kids are off in a playroom,” she says. “My mother always told me to put the drawing table close to where the adults spend their time. Ours is next to our kitchen island, so our kids can draw while we’re cooking.”

#10607. The Hidden Problems Behind Website-to-CRM Integrations (and How to Prevent Them)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Connecting a website form to a customer relationship management (CRM) system may seem straightforward. A developer collects information from a form, sends it to an API endpoint, and checks whether a new contact appears in the CRM.

The integration may work perfectly during the first test. However, problems can appear after the website goes live. Some leads may not reach the CRM, duplicate contacts may appear, or important customer information may be missing.

These issues are not always easy to notice. A visitor might see a confirmation message even when the CRM has failed to save their information.

This guide explains common problems in website-to-CRM integrations and practical ways developers can prevent them.

A website-to-CRM integration allows information collected through a website to move into a CRM system. This usually happens through an API or webhook.

For example, when someone completes a contact form, the website collects their name, email address, phone number, and other details. The integration then sends this information to the CRM, where it can be stored and used by the relevant team.

An API integration provides a structured way for two applications to exchange information. Developers who need additional background can also read OpenHerald's overview of API integration.

The process usually involves several steps:

The website validates the submitted information.

The application sends a request to the CRM.

The CRM checks the request and processes the data.

The website or backend handles the response.

Each step needs to work correctly. If one part fails, the information may not reach its destination.

One important rule is to avoid displaying a successful submission message before the application has safely accepted and stored the data.

Data issues are among the most frequent problems in website-to-CRM integrations. They may not appear during development because test submissions usually contain simple, predictable information.

Real visitors enter data in different formats and may submit the same form more than once.

A visitor might complete a contact form and later download a resource using the same email address. If the integration creates a new CRM record every time, the same person may appear several times.

To prevent this, developers should decide how existing contacts will be identified.

Email addresses are commonly used for matching. Before comparing them, the application should remove unnecessary spaces and convert the address to a consistent format.

These values should be treated consistently.

Where supported, an upsert operation can create a new contact or update an existing one instead of creating unnecessary duplicates.

Website forms and CRM systems do not always use the same field structure.

A website may collect a visitor's full name in one field, while the CRM expects separate first-name and last-name values. Other fields may have different names or requirements.

Developers should create a clear mapping between website fields and CRM fields before building the integration.

They should also check which fields are required. If the CRM requires information that the website does not collect, the request may fail.

Different systems may store information in different formats.

For example, one application might use United Kingdom, while another expects UK. Dates, phone numbers, and country values can also create problems.

A reliable integration should validate and standardise these values before sending them to the CRM.

A contact record is more useful when the sales or marketing team knows where the visitor came from.

However, integrations sometimes send only basic contact information and leave out details such as campaign source, landing page, and referral information.

Developers should identify which tracking fields are useful and include them in the integration where appropriate.

Even an integration that works correctly at launch can stop working later.

Authentication credentials may expire, permissions may change, or an API provider may limit the number of requests an application can make.

Three areas deserve particular attention.

Many APIs use access tokens or other credentials to verify requests. Some tokens expire and must be refreshed.

If an application does not handle token renewal correctly, requests may begin failing without an obvious problem on the website.

Developers should implement the authentication process recommended by the CRM provider and monitor failed requests.

An API provider may restrict the number of requests allowed within a particular period.

A marketing campaign can suddenly increase website traffic and generate more form submissions than usual. If the integration exceeds the provider's limit, some requests may be rejected.

The application should recognise rate-limit responses and retry requests according to the provider's instructions.

An integration should not receive more access than it needs.

For example, a form submission service may only need permission to create or update contacts. Giving it full administrative access increases unnecessary security risks.

Use the minimum permissions required for the integration to function.

External services can experience outages, network delays, and temporary errors. If the website sends a form submission directly to the CRM without storing it first, a failed request could mean a lost lead.

A safer approach is to separate receiving a submission from delivering it to the CRM.

Validate the form information on the server.

Store the submission safely in your own system.

Send it to the CRM through a background process.

Retry temporary failures after an appropriate delay.

Flag permanent failures for manual review.

This approach gives the application another opportunity to deliver information when the CRM becomes available again.

A request might reach the CRM successfully, but the response could be lost because of a network problem. The website may then retry the same request, creating a duplicate contact.

Idempotency helps prevent this situation. The application can use a stable identifier for each submission so that repeating the same operation does not create another record.

For example, a combination of the form ID and a normalised email address may help identify repeated submissions. The exact approach depends on the CRM's API capabilities.

This is an illustrative example. Functions such as crmUpsertContact() and scheduleRetry() need to be implemented according to the application and CRM being used.

The important point is that every submission should have a known status: successfully delivered, waiting for another attempt, or requiring manual attention.

A working integration should also protect the quality and security of the information it collects.

Public forms can receive automated submissions from bots. Without appropriate protection, these entries can fill the CRM with unwanted records.

Validation should happen on the server, even if the website already checks information in the browser.

Some forms collect permission to send marketing communications.

If a visitor selects a consent checkbox, that information should also be passed to the CRM. Otherwise, the CRM may contain the contact details without a reliable record of the visitor's choice.

Where relevant, store the consent value, the wording or version displayed, and the time the visitor gave consent.

An integration should only send the information needed for its intended purpose.

Collecting unnecessary personal details increases the amount of information the application must protect and maintain.

Developers should also understand where submitted information is stored, including databases, queues, application logs, and the CRM.

Testing an integration before launch is important, but monitoring it afterwards is just as necessary.

A successful test does not prove that every future submission will work.

The following checks can help identify problems early.

Compare the number of website form submissions with the number of contacts successfully created or updated in the CRM.

A growing difference between the two numbers may indicate that some requests are failing.

Application logs should record the reason a request failed and include a submission identifier where possible.

Avoid storing complete personal details in logs unless there is a specific, justified need.

Developers should configure notifications when the integration's failure rate exceeds an acceptable threshold.

This makes it easier to investigate problems before they affect a large number of submissions.

A scheduled test submission can help confirm that the complete process is still working.

For example, a test lead can be sent periodically and checked to confirm that it reaches the CRM correctly.

Someone should be responsible for monitoring the integration.

This person or team should review errors, check API changes, monitor credentials, and investigate changes to CRM fields.

Without a clear owner, small problems can remain unnoticed for a long time.

Documentation makes integrations easier to maintain and troubleshoot.

It does not need to be complicated. A short reference document covering the main rules can save considerable time when another developer needs to work on the system.

Before deployment, developers should also test unusual situations.

Testing these situations helps reveal weaknesses that ordinary form submissions may not expose.

What is the most common website-to-CRM integration problem?

Duplicate contacts and incorrect field mapping are common problems. They usually happen when the website and CRM handle data differently.

How can developers prevent duplicate contacts?

Normalise email addresses, use a consistent matching rule, and use an upsert operation or idempotency mechanism where the CRM supports it.

Should a website send form data directly to a CRM?

For more reliable handling, the application should first validate and safely store the submission. A background process can then deliver it to the CRM and retry temporary failures.

How can I tell if a CRM integration has stopped working?

Compare website submission counts with CRM records, monitor failed requests, and schedule regular test submissions.

Who should be responsible for maintaining the integration?

Assign a developer or technical team to monitor the connection, review errors, maintain credentials, and respond to API changes.

Developers can make these integrations more reliable by validating information on the server, storing submissions before delivery, using safe retry mechanisms, and monitoring the results after launch.

The goal is simple: every valid submission should reach the CRM, and every failed submission should be visible and recoverable rather than silently lost.

#10604. A grand new start of it: Exploring Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s effect on business—in New York City and beyond

A democratic socialist running the financial capital of the universe? For a magazine obsessed with how business can change—and change the world—it’s hard to imagine a more intriguing experiment.

As Zohran Mamdani wraps up his first year as New York City’s mayor, we decided to explore a possibility that got lost in the reductive shouting that surrounded his campaign: What if his democratic socialism-fueled agenda is actually good for business? And what will happen as other cities and states elect leaders with similar ideas?

Making New York more affordable is a goal that most of us can get behind. So is making city government faster, more responsive, and more innovative. The question—a thorny one—is whether Mamdani can deliver a more equitable city without throwing a wet blanket over the investment and entrepreneurship that help it thrive.

That tension animates this issue’s cover story, by Morgan Clendaniel, our executive editor, digital. Clendaniel, who has long covered the intersection of business and progressive politics, spoke to Tony Shorris, president and CEO of the NYC Economic Development Corporation, and Julie Su, deputy mayor for economic justice, about the sweeping role that they believe government can play in the economy—speeding up procurement, cutting red tape, making city services function.

The revolution may include city-owned grocery stores. It will definitely include high-tech public bathrooms.

Capitalism + democratic socialism

There’s something invigorating about that combination of grand ambition and attention to the daily details. At Fast Company, we spend a lot of time talking to visionaries who see a broken system and decide to build something better. It’s exciting to see that startup energy coursing through City Hall.

Clendaniel interviewed chief executives, too, such as Warby Parker’s Neil Blumenthal, and he spoke with key opposition figures, including Steven Fulop, president and CEO of the pro-business Partnership for New York City, and the venture capitalist Bradley Tusk. (Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager, had his own words for the mayor at our Innovation Festival in September.)

This unfettered-capitalism crowd worries that the S-word alone is enough to discourage investment in New York and prompt companies to relocate or move jobs elsewhere. There’s some fearmongering here, no doubt, but also some merit. Business hates uncertainty.

These are complex questions worth exploring with an open mind and a willingness to scrutinize the trade-offs. Clendaniel does just that, with a big assist from his editor, Jill Bernstein.

A visual caffeine jolt

Meanwhile, our creative director, Mike Schnaidt, came up with the idea for the coffee cup on the cover, brought to life by illustrator Justin Metz. Along with Clendaniel and Bernstein’s journalism, this graphic effort reminds me why I love making this magazine. Even in the fully digitized, AI-ified year of 2026, a great magazine cover can turn a complicated argument into something immediate and surprising.

Here, an everyday New York object carries an extraordinary question about the future of the city—and the ever-evolving relationship between the private sector and the public good.

#10600. AI’s new business model: Break the internet, then sell the fix

People who work in cybersecurity or work on the fundamentals of digital infrastructure do not want to live in “exciting times,” but right now, they don’t have a choice.

Binance was just hacked in what is, so far, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, narrowly averted a major attack through a third-party extension that would have allowed hackers to upload worms to the affected computers. A number of major airlines were affected when the Spanish travel-tech company Amadeus was hacked, leaking customer information on the web (mercifully without payment info, this time). At the center of this are generative AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which all at once are empowering hackers while billing themselves as the only line of defense. They’ve found a new niche, and it’s to become a protection racket. 

The threat is quantifiable: Severe bugs are classified as CVEs (common vulnerabilities and exposures), and around 400,000 have been officially logged since 1988. Of those, 13,000 happened in the last month. PHP2Shell is the perfect example of this. If you spent any time on social media in the last few weeks, you probably heard some chatter about PHP2Shell and just how dire the threat was. Roughly 70% of websites rely on code written using PHP, and the announcement of a fundamental bug in the language—akin to discovering that millions of buildings share the same faulty lock, potentially giving intruders easy access—had people panicking. Websites such as Wikimedia preemptively went offline until a fix was pushed through.

These bugs were rediscovered separately by two cybersecurity firms: Calif and Wiz. The bugs are very difficult to spot. They had to do with how the host computer accesses memory while an application is running: If a malicious actor forced an out of memory condition by whatever means, it would be possible to interrupt the runtime, leave a partially initialized object behind, and have the application treat it as valid. It would be a stepping stone for a hostile takeover of the host server, while a separate bug could leave instructions from a request that could be read again subsequently instead of being reset. This can be an apocalyptic threat if somebody can actually do those things. They would gain remote control over the host computer, and at that point they can do whatever they want with that machine and what’s on it.

Notably, developers at the PHP Foundation knew about this bug in 2024, but couldn’t agree on a solution for it. Every proposed fix had associated costs, and in any event, nobody actually knew how to act against these bugs. The threat was completely theoretical. It sat there, which wasn’t the optimal workflow, but it also wasn’t an omega-level threat until generative AI came into the picture. Forcing the condition while also creating the takeover wasn’t easy to do. Once the vulnerability was publicly announced, what had been a trickle of attacks became a flood. Fixes were rapidly pushed (in some cases by volunteers) and anybody running a website on PHP was urged to quickly upgrade to protect themselves.

This was just one bug, but pretty much everybody expects that more will be found. The people talking loudest about the danger are, surprisingly, generative artificial intelligence companies. AI companies are all too happy to make clear how incredibly dangerous all of this is and how many more bugs and vulnerabilities they expect to find as they continue to look around. Sam Altman doesn’t think we’ll be able to patch all the bugs, while Jason Clinton of Anthropic terms it a “vulnerability tsunami.” They’re promising years of instability following this as they struggle to discover and patch all of these bugs—an ongoing process, because software development is itself a process of continual updates. 

Why are they talking this way? They’re emphasizing how dangerous their product is, which seems like terrible salesmanship. But they’re also peddling the solution to the problem they helped to introduce.

And to force the issue, they’re going to look for the bugs themselves. That’s the point of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which is all about looking for defects and vulnerabilities in open-source software. Nor are they just running around bug-hunting and letting chaos ensue. They’re trying to step into the cybersecurity space and set themselves up as the best solution to the problem.

OpenAI unveiled a new security-focused model in September, GPT-6 Cyber. OpenAI’s Daybreak program is intended to be available only to eligible organizations so that only “good actors” can take advantage of this, though in the long term as models become open access it’s not clear how that distinction will matter. Anthropic has its own model, Claude Mythos Preview. Google has Gemini Carbon 4 as its cybersecurity model. As with all models, you pay per token. Access to Daybreak is subsidized, although if you’re a believer in Cory Doctorow’s theory of enshittification, the long-term business model will be to make this more expensive over time as customers grow to depend on it. These companies are desperate for new sources of revenue even as overall revenue growth slows.

They’re not being subtle about this. Sam Altman told a group of business students at Stanford that “I think we’re going to have to completely switch the defense model to using the same technology for a new kind of defense shield.” In other words: Gotta use my products to keep yourself safe. What they’re doing verges on extortion; they’re trying to monetize the chaos their products are introducing. But in addition to that, they’re taking aim at a fundamentally vulnerable digital space.

A threat to the open-source commons

Let’s take a step back and consider how the internet, much of which runs on open-source software, is really maintained. PHP is supported by the PHP Foundation, which has just over a dozen employees and relies on donations. It is in effect a passion project for a few developers. There’s an Xkcd comic that sheds a great deal of light on this: Random critical pieces of digital infrastructure are being maintained by people entirely on their own, thanklessly and often without compensation. The modern open internet has been built up in ad hoc ways that often deprioritized security, but that mattered less when only human beings were doing the building or the hacking. To take advantage of those vulnerabilities would require not just expertise, but a great deal of time, effort, and computational power in many cases. PHP2Shell’s exploits were hard to spot, even if you really knew what you were doing and understood PHP down to the source code.

Yes, these potential threats are dire, but this isn’t a tsunami or a natural disaster that simply could not have been prevented. This is entirely manmade, and the people shrieking about what a dire emergency it is are also the ones who have helped to inaugurate it. This exploit sat virtually unknown by anybody for more than a decade, and even when it was recognized for what it was, the threat was purely theoretical. Now because of generative AI, cybersecurity is starting to favor the attack rather than the defender. People like Sam Altman helped to create the problem, first by developing the models, and now by going around and actively looking for weak points in our ramshackle internet. They broke it, and now they’re here to offer a solution: “Nice open internet you’ve got right there; it would be a shame if something happened to it.”

And what are the costs associated with this? For individual consumers of course, there’s the threat of hacks, theft, and general instability on the internet. For businesses, outages, lost revenue, and theft. That’s severe. But I think that there’s a more fundamental risk to the whole of the internet, at least as we know it. Groups like the PHP Foundation or the individual developers who sustain free and open-source software (FOSS) are going to be under even greater strain in the years to come, especially when compared to companies like Anthropic that, for the moment at least, have very deep pockets. Those 13,000 CVEs I mentioned at the beginning of the piece? Those largely fall on volunteers and overworked organizations to remediate, which will burn them out and in the long run likely push people away from the whole FOSS project. 

Turning to generative AI is probably what Anthropic and every other company wants, as another use case for their products, but it poses its own severe risks. Large language models (LLMs) are already being used on open-source projects that call into question the whole license-free structure and system of attribution that has made FOSS possible. That’s one leg of our stool that’s being kicked out from under us.

On top of that though, as AI-generated code winds up in more FOSS projects, is it going to introduce more vulnerabilities that will then have to be hunted down and eliminated? The answer seems to be yes. Whether it’s from vibe coding or simply the fact that LLMs trained on code with security vulnerabilities will tend to reproduce those vulnerabilities, we’re likely going to be running in place for years on end. And even if it can be introduced without undermining the security of the code itself, it’s another avenue to eat away at the licensure and copyright-free status that makes FOSS possible.

So this protection racket that’s forming is more than just a tax. It’s going to massively destabilize the ecosystem of the internet as we know it. I don’t know what comes next if the delicate FOSS sandbox falls apart. Maintainers could abandon their projects, which in turn creates more security vulnerabilities as things fall out of date and become obsolete. Even stably running pieces of infrastructure will eventually be unsupported by the languages that they run on; people can wake up one morning and find that some odd dependency powering their website stopped working. Who’s responsible at that point for fixing it? 

Nor do I want to see it entrusted to for-profit entities. Maintaining this work is basically thankless as it stands; it’s unprofitable to take on because the whole point is that everybody can freely use it. The only reason for them to do so in the long run would be to monetize it, which costs the rest of us. And as they make these into their own proprietary systems, will they wall off what is theirs from everything else? Why shouldn’t they; Microsoft spent years fighting the FOSS movement because it saw open-source software as a threat to its copyrighted systems. What has been up until now a true commons, maintained by people and organizations largely doing it out of passion, would become something else entirely: less able to talk to each other, and more expensive to use.

What’s the solution? This is probably a whole other essay, but in the long run it’s going to have to be government. Whether by directly assuming the burden or offering cash and resources to private groups, governments need to take steps to ensure that an open and free internet continues to exist. Could something like the United Nations do it, ensuring that it’s a truly global movement instead of under one national or regional umbrella? Failing that, could the European Union take it on—a prudent move, especially as Europe tries to get out from under the thumb of U.S. big tech. Food for thought, because under the shadow of all of these scary cyberattacks, that’s where I think the real threat lies.

As high-end PC hardware continues to surge in demand and price, GPU theft has become a highly profitable target for criminals. According to a report by ABC7 News, authorities are investigating a major cargo heist involving the disappearance of an $11.4 million shipment of Nvidia hardware. The shipment reportedly consisted of six pallets of Nvidia hardware that left Oakland for Texas on August 29 and was picked up by a truck posing as a food transport company. Investigators eventually lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County, with the Oakland Police Department receiving a report of the theft on September 13.

"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," said Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business.

While there has been no announcement regarding any arrests, the authorities are said to be investigating the matter. The incident has also raised concerns among experts about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security risks posed by advanced computing hardware making its way into black-market channels.

In a similar incident from Brazil back in September, two pallets containing Nvidia's top-of-the-line GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards, valued at approximately $470,000 (R$2.5 million), disappeared at Guarulhos International Airport in São Paulo. The shipment, imported from the US, had reportedly arrived at the airport on September 20 and cleared customs on September 24, but the two pallets went missing the following day after being authorized for release.

The investigation eventually uncovered a possible inside job, with Brazilian police identifying three airport employees suspected of helping carry out the heist. According to reports, two outsourced forklift operators allegedly removed the pallets from a warehouse, an incident that was reportedly captured on CCTV, while a third employee responsible for checking and releasing merchandise allegedly helped bypass the airport's electronic controls.

Things took an interesting turn when one of the stolen Zotac RTX 5090 graphics cards appeared for sale on the Brazilian online marketplace OLX for more than $6,000. The listing included clear pictures of the card's serial number, allowing it to be linked to the missing shipment. The listing has since been taken down, while the whereabouts of the remaining graphics cards remain unclear.
